P0E00.d: P0E00 is the general circuit code for the current sensor in phase U of the generator. Each phase sensor, usually a Hall-type device inside the inverter, outputs a voltage around a mid-point when no current flows.
s: Hybrid system warning and engine warning light
Generator switched off, reduced performance
Vehicle may not reach ready mode
c: Supply or reference fault of the current sensor
Defective phase U current sensor inside the inverter
Faulty internal connection between sensor and control board

P0E01.d: P0E01 flags an implausible zero point of the U-phase current sensor inside the generator inverter. Sensors of this kind put out a voltage near the middle of their span while no current flows, so the test is only run when the machine cannot carry current.
s: MIL and hybrid system warning light on
Generator output reduced, less charging while driving
Code often returns after clearing at the next standstill check
c: Zero point of the phase U current sensor drifted (sensor inside the power drive unit)
Unstable sensor supply or reference voltage inside the inverter
Evaluation circuit of the generator control unit faulty

P0E02.d: P0E02 is stored when the output of the generator inverter's phase U current sensor falls to the bottom of its range, a level no real current would produce. Mitsubishi uses it on the Outlander PHEV: from model year 2023 the generator control unit, supplied with at least 8 V, sets P0E02-00 once the U-phase signal drops to 0.5 V or lower and stays there for 0.2 s; unlike the zero-point test, no standstill is needed.
s: MIL and hybrid system warning light on
Generator power limited or generator not used
Battery charge falls faster in hybrid operation
c: Sensor signal shorted to ground or sensor output failed low
Open signal or supply connection of the sensor inside the power drive unit
Input stage of the generator control unit faulty

P0E03.d: P0E03 is the upper-limit fault of the current sensor that measures phase U of the generator inverter: its signal is pinned near the supply rail. In the 2023 Outlander PHEV, Mitsubishi lets the generator control unit set P0E03-00 when the U-phase voltage climbs to at least 4.5 V and remains there for 0.2 s with the unit supplied by at least 8 V; for the 2018 model the code list blames a short to the supply or a shorte
s: MIL and hybrid system warning light on
Generator switched off or strongly limited
Engine runs more often without charging the battery
c: Sensor signal shorted to its supply voltage
Current sensor in the power drive unit failed with high output
Lost sensor ground or reference inside the inverter

P0E04.d: P0E04 is the general circuit code for the generator inverter's V-phase current sensor, meant for an electrical fault that is not narrowed down to offset, low or high. No manufacturer documents P0E04 publicly.
s: Hybrid or engine warning light on
Reduced generator output
c: Electrical fault in the V-phase sensor circuit inside the inverter
Poor contact at the inverter or generator control unit connector

P0E05.d: P0E05 reports an implausible zero point of the current sensor in phase V of the generator inverter. Mitsubishi describes it only for the 2023 Outlander PHEV, the first of its generator units with a sensor in phase V; the earlier model measured just U and W.
s: MIL and hybrid system warning light on
Possibly also the phase sum code P0DFA stored
Less generator support during hybrid driving
c: Zero point of the phase V current sensor drifted
Disturbed sensor supply or reference in the power drive unit

P0E06.d: P0E06 means the phase V current sensor of the generator inverter delivers a signal at the floor of its range. The 2023 Outlander PHEV is the only documented user: Mitsubishi's generator control unit, running on 8 V or more, stores P0E06-00 when the V-phase voltage remains at 0.5 V or below for 0.2 s, and the MIL comes on.
s: MIL and hybrid system warning light on
Generator power limited
c: V-phase sensor signal shorted to ground or sensor failed low
Open sensor signal or supply inside the power drive unit
Input of the generator control unit faulty

P0E07.d: P0E07 is set when the phase V current sensor in the generator inverter reports a signal stuck high. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV has its generator control unit flag P0E07-00 as soon as the V-phase voltage is at 4.5 V or above for 0.2 s while its own supply is at least 8 V; MIL and hybrid warning both illuminate.
s: MIL and hybrid system warning light on
Generator switched off or limited
Other phase current sensor codes stored at the same time
c: V-phase sensor signal shorted to its supply
Common sensor supply in the power drive unit too high or faulty
Current sensor failed with high output

P0E08.d: P0E08 covers an electrical fault of the generator inverter's W-phase current sensor that falls outside the offset, low and high categories. No manufacturer documents P0E08 publicly.
s: Hybrid or engine warning light on
Reduced generator output, battery charged less while driving
c: Electrical fault in the W-phase sensor circuit inside the inverter
Loose or corroded connector at the power drive unit

P0E09.d: P0E09 is the zero-point check of the phase W current sensor in the generator inverter. Mitsubishi uses it on two Outlander PHEV generations.
s: MIL and hybrid system warning light on
Rough or reduced generator operation
Fault reappears at the next standstill check after clearing
c: Zero point of the phase W current sensor drifted
Sensor supply or reference in the power drive unit unstable
Evaluation in the generator control unit faulty

P0E0A.d: With P0E0A the phase W current sensor of the generator inverter reports a signal at or near zero volts. Mitsubishi covers this code in its Outlander PHEV service information: the 2018 chart attributes it to a short to ground or an open circuit of current sensor 2, and in the 2023 model the generator control unit sets P0E0A-00 after the W-phase voltage has stayed at 0.5 V or lower for 0.2 s with at least 8 V supply, l
s: MIL and hybrid system warning light on
Generator largely out of operation
Battery is charged noticeably less while driving
c: W-phase sensor signal shorted to ground or sensor failed low
Open sensor signal or supply inside the power drive unit
Input stage of the generator control unit faulty

P0E0B.d: P0E0B marks a phase W current sensor signal in the generator inverter that sits at the top of its range. In the 2023 Outlander PHEV, Mitsubishi's generator control unit records P0E0B-00 when the W-phase voltage stays at no less than 4.5 V over a period of 0.2 s with a supply of at least 8 V, and turns on the MIL; the 2018 code chart names a short to the supply or a short circuit of current sensor 2.
s: MIL and hybrid system warning light on
Generator switched off or limited
c: W-phase sensor signal shorted to its supply voltage
Current sensor in the power drive unit failed with high output
Lost sensor ground or reference inside the inverter

P0E0C.d: P0E0C concerns the three power phases between generator inverter and generator, not the current sensors. The J2012 title fits the use Mitsubishi documents for the 2023 Outlander PHEV under its own label of generator current deviation: with at least 50 A commanded, the generator between 500 and 4,500 rpm and 8 V supply, a U, V or W current stuck within about 17 A either side of zero for 0.4 s, or a failed comparison w
s: MIL and hybrid system warning light on
Generator no longer charges, engine runs without series hybrid support
Possible noise or vibration from the generator under load
c: Loose or burnt high-voltage phase terminal between inverter and generator
Phase cable or generator winding interrupted
Power drive unit does not drive one phase (switch or driver fault)

P0E0D.d: P0E0D is the low member of the generator phase circuit group: a U, V or W line between inverter and generator is pulled toward the negative high-voltage rail or to ground, for instance through damaged insulation or a lower power switch that conducts when it should not. No manufacturer documents P0E0D publicly.
s: Hybrid system warning light, possibly with insulation fault message
Generator shut down
c: Phase cable or winding insulation damaged, leakage to ground
Lower IGBT of one phase leaking or shorted
Phase voltage evaluation in the inverter faulty

P0E0E.d: P0E0E reports a generator phase line that reads high: one of the U, V or W connections is held near the positive high-voltage potential, typically by an upper power switch that stays on or by a short to the positive rail. No manufacturer documents P0E0E publicly; the generator units Mitsubishi describes for the Outlander PHEV only use P0E0C here, and in GM's tables only the open-phase check P0C05 is used for the corr
s: Hybrid system warning light and MIL on
Generator shut down, no charging while driving
c: Upper IGBT of one phase shorted or not switching off
Phase line shorted to the positive high-voltage rail
Phase monitoring in the inverter faulty

P0E0F.d: P0E0F is set when the generator inverter loses one of its internal supplies, supply A, or the line to it is interrupted. Which supply carries the letter A is up to the manufacturer; usually it is the low-voltage feed of the gate drivers that switch the power transistors.
s: Hybrid system warning light and MIL on
Generator out of operation, vehicle may not reach ready state
c: Gate driver supply inside the inverter failed
12 V feed, fuse or connector of the inverter interrupted

P0E10.d: P0E10 means supply A of the generator inverter is present but too low. Ford lists the code in the HEV OBD system summary for its power-split hybrids (OBDSM1901): in the paragraph on the gate signal lines of motor and generator, P0E10 appears with P0BCE and P0BCF among the generator-side open-circuit faults, while the motor side is covered by P0C0C.
s: Hybrid system warning light and MIL on
Generator limited or switched off, reduced hybrid performance
c: Gate drive supply or gate signal path in the inverter faulty (Ford)
Low 12 V supply to the inverter, e.g. weak battery or poor ground

P0E11.d: P0E11 is stored when supply A of the generator inverter is above its permitted range. Overvoltage on the gate driver feed can overstress the control inputs of the power transistors, so controllers usually react by blocking the inverter.
s: Hybrid system warning light and MIL on
Generator blocked, no charging while driving
c: Voltage regulator of the gate driver supply in the inverter faulty
Short between two internal supply rails
Overvoltage in the 12 V system (DC/DC converter or charging fault)

P0E12.d: P0E12 concerns the command circuit of battery coolant heater A, the electric element that warms the coolant sent to the hybrid or EV battery when the pack is too cold for charging or full power. The controller flags it when this circuit is open or otherwise electrically faulty.
s: Check engine light on
Slow or reduced charging in cold weather
Engine runs more often than usual on cold days
Reduced electric power until the pack warms up
c: Broken or chafed wire in the heater A command circuit
Loose, corroded or unlocked connector at the heater or controller
Open circuit inside the heater A assembly
Failed output driver in the controlling module

P0E13.d: P0E13 is the low-signal case on the command line of battery coolant heater A: the controller reads the line near ground at a moment when it expects a higher level, which points to a short to ground or a driver that cannot pull the circuit up. No manufacturer documents P0E13 publicly.
s: Check engine light on
Battery heater does not work at low temperatures
Longer charging times in winter
c: Command wire shorted to ground, e.g. chafed against the body
Moisture or coolant in the heater connector
Internal short in the heater's control input
Output driver in the controller stuck low

P0E14.d: P0E14 is logged when heater A's control wire sits too high, typically because it touches a supply voltage or because a pulled-up input has lost its connection. No manufacturer documents P0E14 publicly; GM's 2016 Volt reports open, ground and voltage faults of its heater transistor together as P1EC3 (Type B).
s: Check engine light on
Heater shut down by its own overheat protection
Battery heating unavailable or erratic in cold weather
c: Command wire shorted to a supply or neighbouring live wire
Open connection on a pulled-up heater input reading as high
Output driver in the controller that will not switch off

P0E15.d: P0E15 means heater A can be addressed electrically but does not deliver the heat it was asked for. Stellantis uses the code on Chrysler Pacifica plug-in hybrids from 2017 onward and the 2021–2023 Jeep Wrangler 4xe for the high-voltage electric coolant heater (ECH), a LIN-controlled unit that on these models heats the cabin loop.
s: Check engine light on
Message that electric mode is unavailable, engine keeps running
Little or no heat from the electric heater
Permanent code may block an emissions inspection
c: Low coolant, leaks or trapped air in the heater loop
Hybrid control software that needs an update (Stellantis HCP/AHCP)
Heater unit permanently locked or internally failed
Faulty auxiliary coolant pump or restricted hoses
High- or low-voltage supply fault or LIN bus problem at the heater

P0E16.d: P0E16 is the open-circuit code for a second battery coolant heater, B. Why a car has two: some thermal systems pair the pack heater with another heater, for example one for the cabin loop, and can route its heat to the battery.
s: Check engine light on
Battery warms up slowly in cold weather
Reduced charging power at low temperatures
c: Broken wire in the heater B command circuit
Loose or corroded connector at heater B
Open element or electronics inside heater B

P0E17.d: P0E17 reports that the command signal to battery coolant heater B stays too low, most often from a short to ground between controller and heater. No manufacturer documents P0E17 publicly.
s: Check engine light on
Second heater does not support battery warm-up
Slower charging in winter
c: Heater B command wire shorted to ground
Water or coolant in the heater B connector
Internal short at the control input of heater B

P0E18.d: P0E18 says the command line of battery coolant heater B reads high when the controller expects it low, for example from contact with a supply wire or an interrupted pulled-up input. No manufacturer documents P0E18 publicly.
s: Check engine light on
Heater B switched off by its overheat protection
Battery heating unavailable in cold weather
c: Heater B command wire shorted to a voltage source
Interrupted pulled-up input at heater B

P0E19.d: P0E19 means heater B is commanded and electrically intact but the expected warming does not follow. No manufacturer documents P0E19 publicly.
s: Check engine light on
Battery stays cold for a long time after a cold start
Reduced charging and drive power in winter
c: Air pocket or low coolant level in the battery loop
Heater B element producing too little heat
Weak pump, restricted hose or coolant valve in the wrong position
Inlet coolant temperature sensor reading wrongly

P0E1A.d: P0E1A reports an open or otherwise faulty command circuit for battery coolant pump B, a second electric pump found where the battery loop is split or a separate circuit feeds a chiller or heater. No manufacturer documents P0E1A publicly.
s: Check engine light on
Battery or electronics temperatures rise faster under load
Reduced power or charging rate
c: Broken wire in the pump B command circuit
Loose or corroded connector at pump B
Failed pump output in the controlling module

P0E1B.d: P0E1B narrows a pump B command fault down to a level below the expected window, normally because the control or PWM wire has a ground fault, or because a driver that cannot raise it. No manufacturer documents P0E1B publicly.
s: Check engine light on
Pump B does not run
Power limited when the components it cools get hot
c: Pump B control or PWM wire shorted to ground
Coolant or water in the pump connector
Control module software fault, as seen by Ford on the pump A sibling
Internal short at the pump B control input

P0E1C.d: P0E1C is set when the command signal to battery coolant pump B stays above what the controller allows, for instance because the line is shorted to battery voltage or, on a pulled-up PWM input, interrupted. No manufacturer documents P0E1C publicly.
s: Check engine light on
Pump B runs constantly or not at all
Reduced power under heavy load
c: Pump B control wire shorted to battery voltage
Interrupted pulled-up PWM input at the pump
Control module software fault, as Ford found for pump A

P0E1D.d: P0E1D says pump B accepts its command electrically but the effect the controller looks for does not appear, such as the expected flow, speed or temperature change in its loop. No manufacturer documents P0E1D publicly.
s: Check engine light on
Battery or electronics temperatures higher than normal
Gurgling noise from the coolant loop
Power or charging rate limited
c: Air trapped in the loop after a coolant service
Worn pump B or debris blocking its impeller or inlet
Low coolant level or leak in the battery loop
Coolant temperature sensor giving an implausible value

P0E1E.d: P0E1E does not describe the wire or the pump directly but the switching stage that drives pump B: that driver has reported excess current or overheating and has protected itself. Such smart switches measure their own state; a TI automotive high-side switch, for example, turns off at about 150 °C junction temperature or on reaching its current limit and signals the fault on a diagnostic pin.
s: Check engine light on
Pump B switches off intermittently
Battery or electronics temperature rises, power is limited
c: Pump B binding or seized, drawing too much current
Partial short in the pump motor or its wiring
Driver in the module overheating due to location or poor cooling
Degraded output driver in the control module

P0E1F.d: P0E1F reports that the output stage switching battery coolant pump A has hit its current or temperature limit. Ford uses the code on its 2020 hybrids.
s: Check engine light on
Battery coolant pump stops intermittently
Hybrid power limited when the battery gets warm
c: Battery energy control module software (Ford 2020 hybrids)
Pump A binding or seized and drawing excess current
Partial short in the pump motor or harness
Output driver overheating in the module

P0E20.d: P0E20 points at the driver that powers coolant control valve A: its output has exceeded a current limit or run too hot and switched itself off. No manufacturer documents P0E20 publicly.
s: Check engine light on
Valve A stays in its last position
Battery runs too warm or too cold, power or charging limited
c: Valve A sticking or jammed so the actuator stalls
Partial short in the valve actuator motor or its wiring
Degraded valve driver in the control module

P0E21.d: P0E21 is the overload or overheat report of the driver for coolant control valve B. No manufacturer documents P0E21 publicly.
s: Check engine light on
Coolant routing does not change as commanded
Battery temperature drifts, power or charging limited
c: Valve B binding so its actuator stalls against the stop
Short or low resistance in the valve B actuator or harness
Degraded driver stage in the control module

P0E22.d: P0E22 tells that the driver for a third coolant control valve, C, has protected itself against excessive current or heat. No manufacturer documents P0E22 publicly, and none of the reviewed GM, Ford, Stellantis or Mercedes documents uses a valve C at all.
s: Check engine light on
One branch of the coolant loop no longer switches
Battery overcooled in winter or kept too warm in summer
c: Valve C stiff or jammed by deposits
Shorted turn in the valve C actuator motor
Degraded driver stage in the control module

P0E23.d: P0E23 is the catch-all circuit code of drive motor inverter temperature sensor G, a thermistor that watches the power switches of the motor inverter. It stands for an electrical fault the controller cannot pin down as low, high or erratic.
s: Hybrid system warning light and MIL on
Reduced electric drive power
c: Temperature sensor or sensing board inside the inverter failed
Poor contact at an internal or external inverter connector
Faulty evaluation input in the motor control unit

P0E24.d: P0E24 is the plausibility test of inverter temperature sensor G: the signal is electrically fine, but the temperature it reports does not fit. Mitsubishi uses the code on the 2023 Outlander PHEV for IGBT sensor number 7 in the front motor control unit, labelled U-phase H2.
s: MIL and plug-in hybrid warning light on
Often no noticeable change in driving
c: Sensor G reads offset against the other IGBT sensors
Fault on the sensing circuit of the power drive unit
Uneven inverter cooling, e.g. air in the coolant circuit

P0E25.d: P0E25 means the voltage of inverter temperature sensor G has fallen below its valid window. In the 2023 Outlander PHEV, Mitsubishi assigns it to the U-phase H2 sensor of the front motor control unit and sets P0E25-00 once that signal does not rise above 1.25 V during 0.08 s with a unit supply of 8 V upward; the MIL is switched on together with the hybrid warning lamp.
s: MIL and hybrid warning light on
Motor power limited as if the inverter were overheating
c: Sensor signal shorted to ground inside the inverter
Damaged sensing board, e.g. after coolant ingress

P0E26.d: P0E26 is logged when the signal of inverter temperature sensor G climbs above its permitted range. In the 2023 Outlander PHEV it belongs to the front motor unit's U-phase H2 sensor: at least 3.75 V lasting 0.08 s, with at least 8 V supply to the unit, sets P0E26-00 together with MIL and hybrid warning light.
s: MIL and hybrid warning light on
Reduced electric drive power as a precaution
c: Open sensing line or broken thermistor
Signal shorted to the sensor supply

P0E27.d: P0E27 marks short dropouts or jumps in the signal of inverter temperature sensor G. Between the events the reading is normal again, which is what separates it from the steady faults P0E25 and P0E26.
s: Warning light that comes and goes
Brief drops in electric drive power
c: Intermittent contact at an inverter connector
Cracked solder joint on the sensing board

P0E28.d: Sensor H is the eighth temperature sensor of a drive motor inverter, and P0E28 is its general circuit code for an electrical fault without a more precise low, high or erratic finding. No manufacturer documents P0E28 publicly.
s: Hybrid warning light and MIL on
Limited motor torque
c: Sensor H or its sensing board in the inverter failed
Connector or internal wiring fault in the inverter
Evaluation input of the motor control unit faulty

P0E29.d: With P0E29 the controller doubts the reading of inverter temperature sensor H although its voltage is valid. On the 2023 Outlander PHEV Mitsubishi uses it for IGBT sensor 8 of the front motor unit, the V-phase H2 position.
s: MIL and hybrid warning light on
Driving usually unaffected
c: Sensor H offset against the other IGBT sensors
Measuring circuit in the power drive unit faulty

P0E2A.d: P0E2A reports that inverter temperature sensor H delivers a voltage below its lower limit. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV assigns the code to IGBT sensor 8 (V-phase H2) of the front motor control unit, triggered by a voltage at or under 1.25 V lasting 0.08 s while the supply is 8 V or higher; the MIL comes on.
s: MIL and hybrid warning light on
Power reduction similar to an overheating inverter
c: Signal of sensor H shorted to ground
Moisture or coolant damage on the sensing board

P0E2B.d: P0E2B is the upper-limit fault of inverter temperature sensor H. Mitsubishi documents it for the 2023 Outlander PHEV, where sensor H is IGBT sensor 8 at the V-phase H2 position of the front motor unit: a signal reaching 3.75 V for 0.08 s while the unit receives 8 V or more sets P0E2B-00, and the function list shows MIL and hybrid warning light for it.
s: MIL and hybrid warning light on
Drive power may be limited
c: Interrupted signal path of sensor H

P0E2C.d: P0E2C covers an unsteady signal from inverter temperature sensor H: it flickers, jumps or drops out for moments and then recovers. That pattern differs from P0E2A and P0E2B, where the voltage stays beyond a limit.
s: Intermittent warning light
Occasional short power reductions
c: Corroded terminal in the sensor circuit
Hairline crack in the sensing board

P0E2D.d: P0E2D is an internal self-test result of the module that supervises the high-voltage pack: the part that measures cell voltages, usually a dedicated monitor chip with its own converter and reference, does not behave as expected. It casts doubt on the measurement itself, not on a cell.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning and MIL on
Reduced power or vehicle not ready to drive
c: Cell monitoring circuit in the battery control module faulty
Software error in the battery control module

P0E2E.d: P0E2E concerns the high-voltage fuse that protects the branch from the battery to on-board charger A. Battery managements usually judge such a fuse by comparing the voltage ahead of and behind it, as Volvo describes for its HV fuses.
s: Electrical system fault message
No AC charging or vehicle does not start
c: False entry from the battery management software (Audi Q5 PHEV)
Fuse opened after a short in the on-board charger or its cable
Faulty voltage measurement at the fuse

P0E2F.d: P0E2F says the battery management has found a second high-voltage fuse open, or believes it has. Several makers use it.
s: Engine does not start, electric driving only (plug-in hybrids)
Vehicle not ready to drive or propulsion warning
MIL or HV drive system warning on
c: Short circuit in an HV consumer on the protected branch
False detection by the battery management or DC/DC wake-up fault
Faulty voltage measurement behind the fuse

P0E30.d: P0E30 is the code for a third fuse in the high-voltage system, after A (P0A95) and B (P0E2F). No manufacturer documents P0E30 publicly.
s: HV system warning message
Consumers on the affected branch without function
c: Short circuit in a consumer on the third fused branch
Faulty voltage measurement behind the fuse
Software error in the battery control module

P0E31.d: P0E31 is the general circuit code of voltage sensor A in a DC/DC converter, the measurement the converter or its controller uses to regulate output voltage. It is used for electrical faults that do not fit the low, high or erratic categories.
s: Warning light and possibly 12 V battery warning
Engine auto-stop disabled or reduced 12 V supply
c: Voltage measurement inside the DC/DC converter failed
Wiring or connector fault on the converter
Poor ground connection of the converter

P0E32.d: P0E32 flags a voltage reading of DC/DC converter sensor A that is electrically valid but does not match a reference. GM's 2025 engine tables (25OBDG03A, ECM) apply it to a converter that holds the 12 V supply steady during auto-starts: in bypass mode the raw output voltage may differ from the ECM run/crank voltage by no more than 2 V, and Type B (two trips) follows once 320 of 400 samples, taken every 12.5 ms, fail.
s: MIL on after two trips (GM)
Red 12 V warning message (Mercedes)
Auto stop/start unavailable
c: Voltage measurement in the converter drifting
Voltage drop on supply, ground or reference wiring
Control software needing an update (FCA, Mercedes)
Weak 12 V battery distorting the comparison during cranking

P0E33.d: P0E33 means the controller reads an implausibly low value from voltage sensor A of a DC/DC converter, typically because the signal wire is shorted to ground. GM documents it in its 2025 engine control tables (25OBDG03A) for a converter that keeps the 12 V network stable while the engine restarts automatically: the raw voltage value 1 must drop below 1 V, and 320 failing samples out of 400 taken every 12.5 ms, about f
s: MIL on after two trips (GM)
Auto stop/start no longer available
Possible 12 V voltage dips during engine restarts
c: Sensor signal wire chafed through to ground
Voltage measurement inside the converter failed
Moisture in the converter connector bridging to ground

P0E34.d: With P0E34 the controller sees a voltage on sensor A of the DC/DC converter that is too high to be real, which points to the signal being shorted to a battery feed or another live wire. In GM's 2025 tables (25OBDG03A) the ECM flags it when raw voltage value 1 exceeds 28 V, far above anything a 12 V converter output should reach.
s: MIL on after two trips (GM)
Engine auto-stop disabled
c: Signal wire shorted to a battery feed or other live circuit
Lost reference ground of the measurement, signal floats high
Faulty measuring circuit in the converter

P0E35.d: P0E35 is reserved for a voltage sensor A signal that jumps or drops out briefly instead of staying wrong: the reading is erratic, but not low or high long enough for P0E33 or P0E34 to mature. No manufacturer documents P0E35 publicly.
s: Warning light that appears and disappears
Start-stop works only now and then
c: Loose or spread terminal in the converter connector
Ground connection that fails under vibration
Cracked solder joint in the converter's measuring circuit

P0E36.d: P0E36 is the catch-all circuit code for the second voltage measurement of a DC/DC converter, sensor B. Where a converter reads both its input and its output, or monitors one rail twice, the second path gets the letter B; FCA names it voltage sensor 2 on the 2021 Ram 1500 eTorque.
s: Warning light, possibly 12 V battery warning
Start-stop disabled or converter output reduced
c: Open sense wire or unplugged connector
Second measuring path inside the converter failed

P0E37.d: P0E37 says that voltage sensor B delivers a believable number which nevertheless disagrees with what the vehicle measures elsewhere. GM's 2025 engine tables (25OBDG03A) check raw voltage value 2 of the converter against the ECM run/crank voltage: in bypass mode a gap above 2 V counts, and 320 failed samples out of 400 at 12.5 ms set a Type B code.
s: MIL on, after one or two trips depending on maker and software
Start-stop unavailable
c: Second voltage measurement in the converter drifting
Voltage drop on supply or ground wiring distorting the comparison
Controller software needing an update (FCA eTorque)

P0E38.d: P0E38 is stored when the second voltage reading of the DC/DC converter, sensor B, sits at the bottom of its scale. GM uses it in the 2025 engine tables (25OBDG03A) with the same limits as on sensor A, only applied to raw voltage value 2: under 1 V, confirmed by 320 of 400 samples taken at 12.5 ms intervals and only checked at 6.6 V battery voltage or more.
s: MIL on after two trips (GM)
Auto stop/start inhibited
c: Sensor B signal wire shorted to ground
Failed second measuring circuit in the converter
Bent or corroded pin in the converter connector

P0E39.d: P0E39 reports that sensor B of the DC/DC converter reads far too high, a pattern GM attributes to a short to battery. The 2025 engine tables (25OBDG03A) set the bar at more than 28 V for raw voltage value 2, again needing 320 failing samples within 400 at 12.5 ms and a battery voltage of at least 6.6 V, with Type B confirmation over two trips.
s: MIL on after two trips (GM)
Start-stop switched off
c: Sensor B signal shorted to a voltage-carrying wire
Open reference ground letting the signal float high
Failed measuring circuit for sensor B

P0E3A.d: P0E3A covers an unsteady signal from voltage sensor B of a DC/DC converter: short spikes, dropouts or noise that never last long enough for the hard low or high codes. Publicly, no manufacturer documents P0E3A.
s: Sporadic warning light, sometimes cleared on its own
Start-stop unavailable from time to time
c: Harness rubbing intermittently where it moves with the engine
Poor terminal tension in the sensor B circuit
Electrical interference on an unshielded sense line

P0E3B.d: P0E3B indicates that the electric pump circulating coolant through the high-voltage battery turns faster than commanded. A pump that suddenly spins too freely has usually lost its load, because it is moving air instead of coolant after a leak, a low reservoir or a poorly bled system.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning
Reduced charging or drive power when the battery warms up
c: Low coolant level or leak, pump running partly dry
Air left in the battery loop after a repair
Faulty pump electronics or speed feedback signal

P0E3C.d: P0E3C is set when the battery coolant pump stays below the speed it has been asked for. GM documents it specifically for the 2024–25 Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray: the battery energy control module (K16) stores P0E3C, and the ECM may add P0A7B to switch on the MIL.
s: MIL on, with P0A7B stored in the ECM (Corvette E-Ray)
Electric front-axle drive limited when the battery gets hot
c: Air trapped around the pump after earlier service (GM 24-NA-160)
Worn pump bearing or debris slowing the impeller
Low supply voltage or poor ground at the pump

P0E3D.d: P0E3D concerns the lamp or LED that shows the state of the pilot connection to the charging station, not the pilot signal itself. Low means the driver circuit reads too little voltage, typically because the line to the LED is shorted to ground.
s: Pilot indicator stays dark when it should light
Charging itself usually unaffected
c: Wire to the indicator LED shorted to ground at the charge port
Faulty output driver in the controlling module

P0E3E.d: P0E3E is the high-side counterpart for the control pilot indicator circuit: the module senses voltage on the LED line when there should be little or none, the classic sign of a short to a supply wire. Publicly, no manufacturer documents P0E3E.
s: Pilot indicator lit or flickering without reason
Misleading charge port light while charging works
c: Indicator wire chafed against a supply wire near the charge port
Output stage in the module stuck on
Water in the charge port connector bridging pins

P0E3F.d: P0E3F reports that the output feeding charge status indicator A sits too low in voltage. That light confirms to the owner that the vehicle is charging, and the expected cause is an LED line touching ground.
s: Charge status light stays off during charging
Charging continues normally
c: LED supply wire pinched or chafed to ground
Failed driver in the controlling module

P0E40.d: P0E40 is logged when the drive circuit of charge status indicator A carries voltage although the light is commanded off, typically because the line touches a live wire. P0E40 has no public documentation from any manufacturer.
s: Charge status light on although nothing is charging
Owner misled about the actual charge state
c: Indicator wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit
Output driver no longer switching off
Moisture bridging pins in the indicator connector

P0E41.d: P0E41 refers to a second charge status light, indicator B, whose driver circuit is pulled too low, usually by a short to ground. Which light carries the letter B is the maker's choice; a lamp at the charge port alongside the dashboard light would be a typical pair.
s: Second charge light (e.g. at the port) stays dark
Main charge indicator and charging unaffected
c: Indicator B wire pinched to ground near the charge port flap
Water ingress into the charge port light assembly

P0E42.d: P0E42 means the driver circuit of charge status indicator B shows voltage at a moment when the light should be switched off, pointing to a short to a supply wire or a driver that stays on. P0E42 appears in no public manufacturer document.
s: Second charge light glowing or flickering when not charging
Charging itself works
c: Indicator B wire touching a live wire at the charge port
Wet or corroded contacts bridging to a supply pin
Output driver for indicator B stuck on

P0E43.d: P0E43 is the module-B counterpart of P0A1D: it reports that a second hybrid/EV powertrain controller has detected an internal failure or can no longer be trusted. Vehicles with two such processors, for example GM's Bolt EV with a second powertrain module labelled K114B (HPCM2), are where the letter B makes sense.
s: MIL and hybrid or EV system warning
Reduced propulsion power or no ready mode
c: Internal processor or memory fault in module B
Supply, ground or internal bus fault at the module

P0E44.d: P0E44 is the basic circuit code for the fifth pack voltage measurement, channel E, which follows channels A to D (P0ABA, P0B14, P0B19, P0B1E) in the code list. The battery controller stores it when this input is electrically unusable, for example open, without a plausible raw value or failing a self-test of its measuring stage, and none of the more specific low, high or erratic codes fits.
s: Hybrid or high-voltage system warning lit
Reduced electric assist or limited battery power
Vehicle may not switch to ready mode
c: Open or unplugged voltage sense lead or connector inside the pack
Faulty measuring stage or input of the battery controller
Blown fuse or open resistor in the sense path

P0E45.d: P0E45 says pack voltage measurement E delivers a value that is electrically valid but does not fit the rest of the battery data. Such a rationality test usually compares the channel with the summed block or cell voltages, or with a second pack measurement.
s: Warning light with reduced hybrid or electric power
Displayed state of charge or range jumps unexpectedly
c: Corroded or loose sense connection adding resistance and skewing the reading
Drifting measuring stage or outdated software in the battery controller
Fault in the reference value, e.g. a block or cell voltage channel

P0E46.d: P0E46 is stored when pack voltage measurement E reads below the lowest value the connected battery could physically present. That points to the measuring path, such as a sense lead shorted to ground, a blown sense fuse or a failed input stage, not to an empty battery.
s: Vehicle does not become ready to drive or drops out of ready mode
Hybrid system warning and MIL lit
Electric drive or engine assist unavailable
c: Sense lead of channel E shorted to ground or chassis
Blown fuse or open resistor in the sense path pulling the reading down
Defective input stage of the battery controller

P0E47.d: P0E47 means pack voltage measurement E reports more voltage than the pack can reach even when fully charged. A sense lead touching a higher potential, a broken divider resistor or a damaged input of the measuring chip are the usual explanations; real overcharging is unlikely when only one channel shows it.
s: MIL and hybrid warning on
Charging or regenerative braking restricted
Electric drive limited or blocked
c: Sense lead of channel E chafed through and touching a higher potential
Broken divider resistor or lost reference in the measuring circuit
Damaged measuring input or software fault in the battery controller

P0E48.d: P0E48 marks pack voltage measurement E as unsteady: the signal jumps, drops out for fractions of a second or changes faster than a battery voltage can, and then returns to normal. Because the fault comes and goes, it is often found only as a stored code after a brief warning.
s: Warning light that comes and goes
Brief losses of electric power, often on rough roads
Stored code without a current fault
c: Loose, pushed-back or corroded terminal on the channel E sense lead
Chafed sense lead that shorts briefly under vibration
Intermittent fault in the battery controller input

P0E49.d: Channel F is the sixth and last pack voltage measurement in this series and comes after channel E (P0E44 to P0E48). P0E49 is its general circuit fault: the battery controller cannot use the input, for instance because the sense line is open, the measuring chip reports an internal error or the raw value is missing, while no clear low, high or erratic pattern applies.
s: High-voltage warning and reduced power
Vehicle may refuse to become ready
c: Open sense lead or disconnected connector of channel F
Internal fault of the voltage measuring chip or battery controller
Moisture or corrosion in the pack-side connector

P0E4A.d: P0E4A reports that pack voltage measurement F lies within its electrical range but disagrees with a reference value. No manufacturer documents P0E4A publicly.
s: MIL on in the first trip with reduced battery power
Implausible state of charge display
c: Contact resistance at a sense terminal distorting the channel F value
Fault in the comparison value, such as the inverter bus or cell voltage measurement
Measuring drift or software issue in the battery controller

P0E4B.d: P0E4B sets when pack voltage measurement F falls below its plausible minimum, which normally points to a sense path shorted to ground, an open sense fuse or a defective input of the battery controller. No manufacturer documents P0E4B publicly.
s: No ready mode or contactors do not close
MIL and high-voltage warning on
c: Channel F sense lead shorted to ground or pack housing
Open fuse or resistor in the channel F sense path
Failed analog input of the battery controller

P0E4C.d: P0E4C means pack voltage measurement F reports a value above anything the battery can produce. Common reasons are a sense line in contact with a higher potential, a lost ground reference in the measuring circuit or a faulty analog input, so the channel rather than the cells is suspect.
s: Warning lamp and limited electric drive
Charging interrupted or not started
c: Channel F sense line touching a higher potential
Lost ground reference or broken divider in the measuring circuit
Faulty analog input or software of the battery controller

P0E4D.d: P0E4D flags pack voltage measurement F as intermittent: short dropouts, spikes or steps that a real high-voltage battery cannot make, followed by normal readings again. Where a vehicle cross-checks several voltage sensors, as GM does in its 2019 hybrids between the pack sensor and the inverter or charger bus (P0AF8), such glitches can also surface as correlation faults.
s: Intermittent warning light
Sporadic power limitation
Additional correlation codes stored
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the channel F sense circuit
Sense lead that loses contact when the harness moves
Interference or intermittent fault in the measuring electronics

P0E4E.d: P0E4E reports that the hybrid system commanded an engine start but the crankshaft did not turn, or did not reach the cranking speed it expected. It differs from P0A0F, where the engine is turned over but does not fire and keep running.
s: Engine does not turn over when the hybrid system calls for it
Vehicle runs electrically only or shows a stop-safely warning
No start at all once the battery is depleted
c: High-voltage battery too low to crank, often after repeated failed starts
Mechanically seized engine or blocked transaxle
Fault in the cranking motor-generator, its inverter or a conventional starter
Crankshaft speed not detected because of a sensor or signal fault

P0E4F.d: P0E4F covers coolant pump A of the motor electronics loop, which cools the inverter and drive motor, and sets when the signal exchanged with the pump becomes unstable rather than permanently open or shorted. Ford uses exactly this code in the OBD summaries for its hybrid and plug-in hybrid models of 2015 to 2019: the pump reports back to the module, and P0E4F is stored when that feedback is outside the expected frequ
s: MIL or hybrid system warning
Power reduction when inverter or motor temperature rises
Fault may clear itself and return later
c: Loose, corroded or wet pins in the pump A connector
Chafed command or feedback wire that loses contact intermittently
Failing electronics inside the pump sending an unstable feedback signal
Unstable 12 V supply or poor ground at the pump

P0E50.d: P0E50 is the intermittent or erratic fault of the control circuit for coolant pump B, the second electric pump some hybrids use in the inverter and motor electronics cooling. No manufacturer documents P0E50 publicly.
s: Warning light that appears now and then
Temporary power reduction under high load or heat
c: Intermittent contact at the pump B connector or a harness splice
Pump B electronics producing an unstable signal
Control module software evaluating the pump signal too strictly

P0E51.d: P0E51 is the general circuit fault of current sensor A in a DC/DC converter, the element that tells the converter's controller how many amps flow through its power stage. The code covers a signal path that is broken in a way the controller cannot sort into low, high or implausible.
s: Hybrid or 12 V battery warning in the instrument cluster
12 V battery is charged poorly or not at all
Reduced electric power or limited hybrid functions
c: Current sensor inside the converter defective (usually not replaceable separately)
Loose, corroded or damaged sensor connection or harness
Fault on the converter control board or its sensor supply
Converter or hybrid control software needs an update

P0E52.d: P0E52 is the plausibility test of current sensor A: the signal is electrically valid, yet the measured current does not fit what the converter is doing. Two makers name it.
s: MIL on, often after only one drive
Limited power with Stop Safely Now or Service Vehicle Soon message
Reduced eTorque assist or start/stop function
c: Control software with unsuitable limits (FCA eTorque HCP update)
Internal fault of the inverter system controller (Ford hybrid)
Current sensor drifting or offset out of tolerance
High resistance at sensor connector or ground

P0E53.d: P0E53 means the signal of DC/DC converter current sensor A sits below its valid window. On a Hall-type sensor with a mid-scale zero point, that usually points to a short to ground, a missing sensor supply or an open signal wire pulled low, not to a real drop in current.
s: Hybrid or charging-system warning lamp
12 V battery discharges because the converter does not supply it
Reduced power or electric drive not available
c: Sensor supply missing or too low
Current sensor or converter electronics defective

P0E54.d: P0E54 reports a current sensor A signal above the range the DC/DC converter accepts. Mercedes-Benz uses it explicitly: its bulletin LI54.10-P-079533, covering the EQB (series 243) and the G-Class including the electric G 580 (series 465), defines P0E5400 as a short to positive of the converter's current sensor A.
s: Red 12 V battery message
White or yellow high-voltage system warnings
Reduced drive power
c: Converter stuck in a fault state after incorrect wake-up (Mercedes 243/465)
Signal line shorted to a supply voltage
Current sensor or converter electronics defective

P0E55.d: P0E55 deals with a current sensor A reading that flickers or vanishes for moments instead of failing for good. FCA documents it repeatedly for the Ram 1500 with eTorque mild hybrid, where the DC/DC converter sits in the 48 V battery pack and is run by the battery pack control module (BPCM).
s: MIL on
12 V battery not charging, flat soon after driving
Limp-home mode and start/stop disabled
c: Battery pack control module software (FCA eTorque, reflash)
Loose or corroded contact in the sensor path
Current sensor or converter electronics failing intermittently

P0E56.d: P0E56 says the voltage arriving at the input of the DC/DC converter, normally the high-voltage bus of the traction battery, is lower than the converter needs to work. Unlike the sensor codes, the reading itself is believed; the supply is the problem.
s: 12 V battery warning, battery discharges while driving
Hybrid system warning, vehicle may not reach ready mode
Reduced power
c: Traction battery deeply discharged or limited by its management system
Main contactor not closing or high-voltage cable/connector fault
Input voltage measurement inside the converter faulty

P0E57.d: P0E57 is set when the DC/DC converter sees more voltage on its input than it is rated for. Excess input voltage stresses the switching transistors and input capacitors, so a converter typically stops working to protect itself.
s: Hybrid system or 12 V battery warning
Converter switches off temporarily, 12 V voltage drops
Reduced power or limited regeneration
c: High-voltage bus driven too high by boost stage, regeneration or charging
Input voltage measurement in the converter reads too high
Hybrid or battery control software needs an update

P0E58.d: P0E58 stands for a general circuit fault of the third temperature sensor in a DC/DC converter, after sensors A (P0C38 ff.) and B (P0C3D ff.). Which part of the converter sensor C watches is up to the maker.
s: Hybrid system warning
Reduced electric assist or power
c: Sensor connection or wiring damaged or corroded
Temperature sensor in the converter defective
Sensor reference or evaluation circuit in the converter faulty

P0E59.d: P0E59 is the best-documented member of this group. Ford's hybrid OBD summaries from 2015 to 2019 assign it to the inductor temperature sensor of the variable voltage converter and monitor it without pause once 500 ms have passed since power-up, provided the 12 V supply lies between 6 and 19 V.
s: MIL on, at FCA after one faulty drive
Reduced hybrid assist or electric driving
Hybrid system warning
c: Inductor temperature sensor drifting, reading off after cold soak
Inductor really overheating, e.g. due to weak electronics cooling
Short or open in the sensor circuit (Ford range limits)

P0E5A.d: P0E5A means the voltage from DC/DC converter temperature sensor C has fallen below its valid window. With the NTC thermistors common in power electronics, a low voltage translates into an implausibly hot reading, so a grounded signal wire or a failed sensor is far more likely than genuine overheating.
s: Hybrid system warning
Converter derated, reduced electric power
c: Evaluation circuit in the converter faulty

P0E5B.d: P0E5B is stored when the signal of DC/DC converter temperature sensor C rises above its valid window. On an NTC circuit with pull-up resistor, that is the typical picture of an unplugged connector, a broken wire or a short to a supply voltage, and it reads as a converter far colder than possible.
s: Hybrid system warning
Power limited as a precaution
c: Connector unplugged or sensor wire broken
Signal shorted to a supply voltage

P0E5C.d: P0E5C flags a sensor C signal that changes faster than the part it watches could heat or cool. A converter inductor or heat sink has thermal mass, so a jump of many degrees within a few milliseconds points to a contact problem in the circuit, not to the converter itself.
s: Hybrid warning that comes and goes
Short episodes of reduced electric power
c: Loose or widened terminal at the sensor or converter connector
Moisture or corrosion in the connector

P0E5D.d: P0E5D adds the intermittent case to the DC/DC converter enable codes P0A11 (open), P0A12 (low) and P0A13 (high). Through the enable line a hybrid or body controller switches the converter on and off; if that line flickers, the converter keeps stopping and restarting.
s: 12 V battery warning that comes and goes
Fluctuating system voltage, flickering lights
Hybrid warning, possibly reduced power
c: Loose or corroded terminal on the enable line
Poor ground reference between controller and converter
Chafed enable wire touching ground intermittently
Output stage in the commanding controller faulty

P0E5E.d: P0E5E reports that the processor of the on-board charger's control unit fails its self-tests. Mitsubishi spells this out for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: P0E5E-00 means a ROM checksum (CRC) error or a RAM read/write error in the charger control; the code lights both the PHEV warning and the MIL.
s: Plug-in charging impossible or interrupted
MIL and hybrid/PHEV warning, sometimes right after charging
c: Control electronics of the on-board charger defective (unit replacement)
Unstable 12 V supply or ground of the charger during start-up

P0E5F.d: P0E5F is not a sensor fault: the coupler temperature sensor A works, but the charging inlet really got too hot. Three makers document it.
s: Charging stops or runs at reduced power
Charge indicator red or flashing red, warning in app or cluster
Charging restarts only after unplugging and replugging
c: Excessive contact resistance in the vehicle charge port (Ford replaces the port)
Worn or damaged plug of the charging cable or station
High ambient temperature or direct sun while charging (Mercedes)

P0E60.d: P0E60 concerns a wired control line that tells the on-board charger which mode to run in, set by the module that coordinates charging. Range/Performance means the line shows a valid level, but its state or response disagrees with the command.
s: Plug-in charging does not start or stops
Charging runs at an unexpected rate
c: High resistance or damage on the mode control line
Input stage of the on-board charger faulty
Output stage or software of the commanding module faulty

P0E61.d: P0E61 means the 12 V enable line that wakes or permits the on-board charger has a circuit fault, most often an open. GM documents it codegenau.
s: Plug-in charging does not start
MIL on after two trips
Battery heating in cold weather may be unavailable
c: Enable wire open or connector at charger/module not seated
Output driver in the controlling module (VICM/HPC2) faulty
Enable input of the on-board charger defective

P0E62.d: P0E62 reports that the enable line of on-board charger A is held at a lower level than its commanded state allows, typically by a short to ground. If the module drives the line high to permit charging, the charger never sees the request.
s: Charging does not start when plugged in
Charging system warning
c: Enable wire chafed and shorted to ground
Enable input of the charger shorted internally
Driver stage in the commanding module faulty

P0E63.d: P0E63 is the high-level counterpart: the enable signal to charger A sits above the level its commanded state allows, for instance because it touches a 12 V feed. In practice the charger may then be woken although no charging is requested, which can drain the 12 V battery while parked, or it may ignore a switch-off command.
s: 12 V battery drained while parked
Charger active or charging not ending as expected
Charging system warning
c: Enable wire shorted to a 12 V supply
Enable input of the charger faulty
Driver stage in the commanding module stuck on

P0E64.d: P0E64 covers an enable line that is electrically intact while the charger still does not respond as it should. Ford documents it in its 2019 hybrid OBD summary, there titled Battery Charger Enable Circuit Range/Performance: the check runs once the charger is in its ready state and the charge wake-up signal Chrg_Wkup has gone high, and it fails when the battery energy control module still reports not ready after 30 se
s: Charging does not start although the cable is connected
Charging system warning or charge port light shows a fault
c: Charger and BECM do not complete start-up within 30 s (software or wake-up timing)
Battery energy control module not waking or not reporting ready
High resistance on the wake-up line producing a marginal level

P0E65.d: P0E65 flags a fault on the wired command line through which the hybrid control unit operates the on-board charger, most often an interrupted line. GM uses it codegenau: in the 2016 Volt the VICM runs the test, in the 2019 hybrid tables (19OBDG01) the HPC2 module.
s: Vehicle does not charge when plugged in
MIL after the second trip with the fault (GM)
Charging fault message in the instrument cluster
c: Broken or disconnected charger control wire
Corroded or pushed-out terminal at charger or control unit
Defective output driver in the commanding control unit

P0E66.d: With P0E66 the controller finds the charger command line pulled lower than the state it is driving, which typically means the wire touches ground somewhere between the control unit and the on-board charger. If the command is active-high, the charger simply never receives it; a grounded line can also overload the output stage that drives it.
s: Charging does not start after plugging in
Charge indicator shows a fault or goes out
c: Control wire chafed through to body ground
Moisture in a connector bridging the signal to ground
Internal short in the charger's command input

P0E67.d: P0E67 is set when the charger command line reads higher than commanded, for instance close to battery voltage while the control unit is holding it off. A short to a live wire is the classic cause; with some driver designs an open line also floats high and lands here.
s: Charging aborted or not offered at all
Charger wakes up or runs without a charging request
c: Control wire shorted to a battery feed or other supply
Open line read as high by the driver circuit
Output stage of the control unit stuck switched on

P0E68.d: P0E68 is the plausibility code of the charger command line: no short or open is present, yet the charger does not react to the command in the expected way or in the expected time. Typical triggers are a charger that wakes too slowly, a voltage drop on the line that leaves the level ambiguous, or software in the two modules that disagrees.
s: Charging starts late, stops or fails intermittently
Charge timer or scheduled charging not working
c: Charger and control unit software not matching
Charger responding late or not at all to the command
Excess resistance in the line distorting the signal level

P0E69.d: P0E69 belongs to the output that drives the small lamp or LED showing the state of the pilot connection to the charging station. Range/Performance means the driver circuit reports a state that does not fit what the module commanded, without a clear short or open.
s: Charge port indicator flickers, stays dark or shows the wrong state
Charging itself usually unaffected
c: Indicator LED aged or partially failed, drawing the wrong current
Loose contact at the charge port lamp connector
Faulty feedback of the LED driver in the control unit

P0E6A.d: P0E6A is the general code for the precharge contactor of the battery charging system. Before the main charging contactors close, this small contactor feeds the charger side through a resistor so the voltage can rise gently towards pack voltage; without it the main contacts would arc.
s: Charging session aborts right at the start
Charging not possible, driving usually still possible
c: Precharge resistor burnt open or overheated
Worn or sluggish precharge contactor in the charging path

P0E6B.d: P0E6B means the precharge contactor of the charging system appears to stay closed although it has been told to open, usually because its contacts have welded. The battery management notices this when the charger side carries voltage before any precharge was requested, or when it does not drop after switch-off.
s: Charging blocked and high-voltage warning displayed
Vehicle may refuse to switch to ready mode
c: Coil kept energised by a control line fault
Residual voltage from another high-voltage unit misread as a closed contactor

P0E6C.d: P0E6C reports that the precharge contactor of the charging system does not close, or that no current flows through the precharge branch, even though the command was given. The charger side then cannot be brought up to pack voltage, the main charging contactors stay open and the session ends before any energy flows.
s: Charging stops a few seconds after plugging in
Repeated clicking from the battery area at charge start
c: Open precharge resistor interrupting the branch
Burnt or contaminated contactor contacts not conducting
Contactor coil not pulling in due to low supply

P0E6D.d: P0E6D concerns the low-voltage side of the charging precharge contactor: the coil circuit through which the control unit switches it, typically interrupted. Unlike P0E6C, which judges what happens on the high-voltage side, this code comes from the driver output itself.
s: Charging cannot be started
High-voltage system fault message
c: Broken coil control wire or unplugged connector
Open winding in the contactor coil
Failed driver stage in the battery management unit

P0E6E.d: P0E6E is stored when the coil circuit of the charging precharge contactor neither shows a clean short nor an open, but its electrical behaviour does not match the command: coil current outside the expected window, a slow pull-in, or feedback that lags behind the switching command. Rising contact resistance in the connector, a coil with changed resistance or a weak supply to the driver are typical.
s: Charging starts only on some attempts
Fault appears mostly in cold weather or with a weak 12 V battery
c: Increased contact resistance in the coil connector
Contactor coil resistance out of specification
Low supply voltage at the contactor driver

P0E6F.d: P0E6F points to the coil control line of the charging precharge contactor sitting too low, most likely shorted to ground. With a high-side driver the coil then cannot be energised, so precharge never starts; the driver itself may shut down to protect itself.
s: Charging does not start, contactor click missing
High-voltage fault message when plugging in
c: Coil control wire shorted to ground inside or near the battery
Shorted turns in the contactor coil
Driver stage switched off by its overcurrent protection

P0E70.d: P0E70 is the high-side counterpart of P0E6F: the coil line of the charging precharge contactor carries voltage although the driver is off. A short to a 12 V feed can energise the coil without a command, which would let the precharge branch conduct unasked; the battery management therefore usually locks out charging.
s: Charging locked out with a high-voltage fault message
Contactor clicks without a charging request
c: Coil control wire shorted to a 12 V supply
Driver stage in the battery management unit stuck on
Open ground return of the coil leaving the line at supply level

P0E71.d: P0E71 compares the torque that the hybrid generator or motor-generator actually provides with the value requested by the hybrid control. If the two drift apart beyond a calibrated margin, the code is set.
s: MIL and service wrench lamp on (Ford)
Reduced power or emergency running mode
Engine runs more often, hybrid assistance missing
c: Fault in the inverter stage feeding the generator
Rotor position sensor (resolver) delivering a wrong angle
Damaged generator winding or internal contamination

P0E72.d: P0E72 refers to the pulse train that an AC charging station places onto the pilot wire. Under SAE J1772, matched by IEC 61851-1, this is a rectangular ±12 V signal at 1 kHz, and its duty cycle tells the car how much current it may draw.
s: AC charging does not start or stops at one station
Charging works normally at other stations
c: Charging station or portable charger generating an off-spec pilot
Faulty charging adapter or extension in the cable path
Pilot measuring circuit in the vehicle charger misreading

P0E73.d: P0E73 is set when the control pilot pulses from the charging station arrive faster than the nominal 1 kHz. Above the permitted band the vehicle can no longer be sure that it decodes the duty cycle, and with it the allowed charging current, correctly; in practice it refuses or ends the session.
s: AC charging refused or stopped shortly after start
Fault tied to a specific station or cable
c: Electrical interference or ringing on the pilot line
Charging station with a faulty pilot oscillator
Damaged charging cable or corroded charge port pin
Faulty pilot input in the on-board charger

P0E74.d: P0E74 reports that the insulation between the cells or internal high-voltage parts of the traction battery and its housing has become too weak, as measured inside the pack. P0AA6, by contrast, covers isolation of the whole high-voltage system.
s: Battery or high-voltage warning lamp on
Vehicle may not enter ready mode or blocks charging
Electric driving disabled
c: Coolant leak or water ingress inside the battery pack
Chafed or damaged insulation of internal high-voltage wiring
Faulty isolation measurement in the battery management

P0E75.d: P0E75 is the basic electrical code for coolant bypass valve A: the control unit finds that the output switching the valve, or the wire leading to it, does not form a closed circuit, in most cases because of an open. Valves of this kind usually divert coolant between loops, for example between the engine and a heater loop that keeps the cabin warm while a hybrid drives electrically.
s: Check engine light
Little or no cabin heat, especially in electric mode
Engine warms up more slowly or runs more often than usual
c: Broken wire or loose connector on the valve A control circuit
Burnt or internally open coil/motor in valve A
Coolant or water ingress corroding the valve connector pins
Faulty output driver in the engine or hybrid control module

P0E76.d: With P0E76 the voltage on the control line of coolant bypass valve A stays lower than the driver expects for its current state, which points to a short to ground somewhere in the harness or inside the actuator. What happens next depends on the driver layout: a low-side output may leave the valve energised all the time, a high-side output can no longer move it at all, and the driver may switch off to protect itself.
s: Check engine light
Valve stays in one position, heating behaves oddly
Possible blown fuse if the short is hard
c: Chafed control wire touching body or engine ground
Internal short in the valve A actuator
Moisture bridging pins in the valve connector

P0E77.d: P0E77 is logged when valve A's drive line carries more voltage than the driver should allow, typically because the wire has rubbed through against a 12 V feed. A low-side driver then sees battery voltage while it is trying to pull the line down and usually reports overcurrent; with some designs an open line can float high and end up here too.
s: Check engine light
Cabin heat unstable or missing
c: Control wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Open circuit that the driver interprets as high

P0E78.d: P0E78 is the plausibility code for the actuator circuit of bypass valve A. Neither an open nor a short is present, yet current, feedback or response time of the actuator do not fit what the module has commanded: a coil whose resistance has drifted, a motor that labours against a sticky shaft, or a supply that sags under load.
s: Check engine light
Heating output varies from trip to trip
c: Deposits or wear making the valve A mechanism sluggish
High resistance at connector or ground of the valve circuit
Low supply voltage to the actuator under load

P0E79.d: P0E79 reports that bypass valve A apparently remains open although the module has asked it to close. The control unit cannot see the valve directly; it infers the position from temperatures, typically by comparing two coolant sensors that should drift apart when the loops are separated.
s: Weak cabin heat in electric mode
Engine starts more often to supply heat
Check engine light
c: Valve A jammed open by debris or a broken internal part
Actuator no longer moves the valve
Hoses swapped at the valve after a repair
Skewed coolant temperature sensor misleading the check

P0E7A.d: P0E7A is the reverse of P0E79: valve A should open and let coolant pass, but the temperature picture says it has stayed shut. Depending on what the valve connects, the result is a loop that gets no flow from the engine side, so heater output or heat transfer drops, or a branch that heats up because it is cut off from circulation.
s: Little or no cabin heat
Rising coolant temperature in the affected loop
Check engine light
c: Debris or deposits blocking valve A
Actuator or gear stuck in the closed position
Air pocket after a coolant service blocking flow

P0E7B.d: P0E7B covers an interrupted control circuit of the second coolant bypass valve, B. The module sees no proper load on its output, so the valve cannot be positioned and stays wherever it last was or springs back to its rest position.
s: Check engine light
Heating or engine warm-up behaves differently
c: Broken wire or unplugged connector at valve B
Internal open in the valve B actuator
Missing supply or ground at a networked valve actuator

P0E7C.d: P0E7C says that the wiring which operates bypass valve B reads too low, typically because a wire or the actuator itself has a ground fault. Stellantis documents the code: bulletin 18-071-26 (revisions A and B, October 2026) for 2025 RAM 1500 pickups fitted with the Hurricane straight-six, SO or HO twin-turbo and bulletin 18-082-26 for the 2025 Wagoneer and Grand Wagoneer name it among the faults cured by new engine c
s: Check engine light
Often no noticeable driving symptom
c: Engine control software needing the update from the manufacturer bulletin (Stellantis 3.0 Hurricane)
Valve B control wire shorted to ground
Internal short in the valve B actuator

P0E7D.d: P0E7D is stored when the line driving valve B sits above its expected level, for instance with the wire chafed against a powered line or a driver that cannot pull the circuit down. Stellantis names this code in the same software bulletins as its low sibling: 18-071-26 for the 2025 RAM pickup with Hurricane power, plus 18-082-26 (SO engine) and 18-083-26 (HO engine) for the 2025 Wagoneer and Grand Wagoneer.
s: Check engine light
Other stored codes after the same software issue
c: Valve B control wire shorted to a voltage source
Open circuit pulled high by the module input

P0E7E.d: P0E7E marks a control circuit of coolant bypass valve B that is electrically intact but does not respond as calibrated: actuator current, feedback or timing lie outside the window the software expects. Stellantis lists P0E7E most often of the valve B codes.
s: Check engine light
Usually no change in driving behaviour
c: Engine control calibration fixed by bulletin 18-106-25 or 18-071-26 (Stellantis)
Valve B actuator moving slowly or not reaching its target

P0E7F.d: P0E7F means coolant bypass valve B is judged to stay open while the module wants it closed. Stellantis documents it on the Chrysler Pacifica plug-in hybrid with the 3.6 litre engine: bulletin 07-008-23 (June 2023) covers cars built from 3 November 2022 to 10 February 2023, where machining debris from the cylinder head water jackets can collect inside the three-way valve.
s: MIL on
Electric drive mode unavailable, engine runs instead
Reduced or unstable cabin heat
c: Machining debris lodged in the three-way coolant valve (Pacifica Hybrid, bulletin 07-008-23)
Worn or broken internals in valve B
Calibration issue addressed by an engine control update (3.0 Hurricane)

P0E80.d: P0E80 reports that bypass valve B has stayed shut although flow through it is requested. Stellantis gives the criterion for the Jeep Wrangler plug-in hybrid (2021 to 2023): the code sets once engine coolant and the inlet of the electric coolant heater differ by more than 40 °F, about 22 K.
s: Check engine light
Intermittent loss of cabin heat
Electric mode may be disabled
c: Hoses at the three-way valve shifted by one port (Wrangler 4xe, bulletin 07-006-23)
Valve blocked by machining debris (Pacifica Hybrid, bulletin 07-008-23)
Valve B actuator seized in the closed position

P0E81.d: P0E81 is the general circuit code for temperature sensor A in an auxiliary cooling loop, a coolant circuit separate from the main engine loop, such as a heater loop of a plug-in hybrid or a loop that cools electric drive parts. The module sees a signal it cannot use at all, without classing it as too low, too high or implausible.
s: Check engine light
Heater or auxiliary pump runs on default values
c: Loose, corroded or unplugged sensor connector

P0E82.d: P0E82 is set when temperature sensor A of the auxiliary cooling loop delivers a clean electrical signal whose value does not make sense against other temperatures. No manufacturer documents P0E82 publicly, but Ford's 2019 hybrid summary spells out such a plausibility test for its heater-loop sensor ECT2 under P2183.
s: Check engine light
Cabin heat regulation off target
c: Sensor A reading drifted out of tolerance
Stuck bypass valve keeping the loops from mixing
Low coolant or air around the sensor tip

P0E83.d: P0E83 means the signal voltage of temperature sensor A in the auxiliary cooling loop has fallen below its valid floor. Coolant sensors are normally NTC thermistors whose resistance drops as they warm, so a low voltage reads as extremely hot coolant.
s: Check engine light
Coolant pump or fan running continuously
Implausibly high temperature shown on a scan tool
c: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Genuinely very hot coolant in the auxiliary loop

P0E84.d: P0E84 is the high-voltage case for sensor A of the auxiliary loop: the signal sits near the reference voltage, which an NTC thermistor would only produce at extreme cold. Far more often the circuit is open, from an unplugged connector, a broken wire or a sensor with an internal break, or the signal line is shorted to a voltage source.
s: Check engine light
Scan tool shows the loop at minimum temperature
Less precise cabin heating
c: Unplugged connector or broken sensor wire
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source

P0E85.d: P0E85 reports that the second charger stage or second on-board charger, labelled B, has become hotter than its own protection limit allows. Like the A counterpart P0D24, it is a heat verdict, not a sensor fault: the charger trusts its reading and cuts back power or stops to save its semiconductors.
s: AC charging slows down noticeably or stops before the battery is full
Charging fault message or flashing charge-port indicator
c: Too little coolant or air flow through charger B (low coolant, pump, blocked fins)
Internal defect in the power stage of charger B
Long full-power charging in very hot surroundings

P0E86.d: P0E86 means charger B sees less voltage at its input than it needs to work, although charging has been requested. It mirrors P0D27, which carries no letter and is used for the first charger.
s: AC charging does not start or stops shortly after starting
Charging works at another socket or station
c: Weak supply at the socket or charging station, long or undersized house wiring
Faulty charging cable, adapter or extension lead
Worn or burnt contacts in the charge inlet or its wiring to the charger
Voltage measurement inside charger B reads too low

P0E87.d: P0E87 flags an input voltage for charger B above what the charger accepts. Ford uses the code in its plug-in hybrid OBD summary (OBDSM1901) in an unusual way: it is part of a plausibility test run on the battery controller (BECM) and judges the charging voltage request that reaches the charger.
s: Charging is refused or ends early
Amber wrench lamp in the instrument cluster (Ford)
c: Implausible charging voltage request from the battery control module (Ford logic)
Software fault in the charger or battery control module
Real overvoltage from the supply or charging station

P0E88.d: P0E88 is set when charger B takes in less current than it should for the charging power it is asked to deliver, with voltage present. Its counterpart without a letter is P0D29.
s: AC charging takes much longer than usual
Charging stops or a charging fault is shown
c: Charger B power stage does not reach the requested power
High resistance at inlet contacts or in the charging cable
Charging station or cable signals a lower current limit than expected

P0E89.d: P0E89 reports more input current into charger B than permitted, and it is the best documented code of this series. Toyota lists P0E8919 on 2021 to 2023 RAV4 Prime XSE models with the 6.6 kW charger, together with P0D2A19 and PFC boost faults; the MIL is on, plug-in charging fails and the charger assembly is replaced (T-SB-0067-22).
s: MIL or EV system warning lamp on
Plug-in charging stops or does not work at all
Vehicle does not start after DC fast charging (Mercedes)
c: Defective power factor correction or power stage in the charger (Toyota RAV4 Prime)
Calibration or software of the vehicle or charging control unit (Isuzu VCU, Mercedes DC charging unit, Ford request logic)
Current ripple or overcurrent from the charging station (Mercedes)

P0E8A.d: P0E8A concerns the measurement, not the current itself: the sensor that tells charger B how much current enters at its input delivers no usable signal. It is the general circuit code; range, low and high faults of the same sensor sit at P2D85, P2D83 and P2D84, and the sensor of charger A uses P0D38.
s: AC charging does not start or is aborted
Charging fault indication; driving remains possible
c: Current sensor or its evaluation inside charger B defective
Open or shorted sensor wiring where the sensor is external
Charger software misjudges the sensor signal

P0E8B.d: P0E8B covers an electrical fault in the voltage measurement at the input of charger B: the controller gets no valid reading of the supply voltage. Range, low and high faults of this sensor have their own codes, P2E84, P2E85 and P2E86; charger A uses P0D3D for its first input voltage sensor.
s: Plug-in charging is not possible
Charging fault message or charge-port indicator signals a fault
c: Voltage sensing circuit inside charger B defective
Loose or corroded connector, damaged sensing lead

P0E8C.d: The inverter of drive motor A may measure its high-voltage DC level at more than one point; sensor B is the second of those channels. P0E8C is the general circuit code for it, used when the signal is missing or electrically invalid without a clear low, high or plausibility verdict.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning together with the MIL
Reduced electric drive power or vehicle not ready to drive
c: Sensing circuit for voltage channel B inside the power electronics defective
Low-voltage connector or harness of the inverter loose or damaged
Software fault in the motor control unit

P0E8D.d: P0E8D says that voltage sensor B of the drive motor A inverter delivers a value that is electrically fine but disagrees with other readings of the same bus. Mitsubishi details the check for the 2023 Outlander PHEV, where sensor B is the main channel at capacitor 2 (V2M): with the boost converter switched off and the unit powered with 8 V or more for 0.5 s, a gap of at least 100 V to the rear motor unit, or of at leas
s: Red high-voltage system warning at start, stop safely (Audi)
MIL and hybrid warning, reduced or no electric drive
c: Fault in the power electronics or its voltage measurement (Mitsubishi, Audi)
Drift of voltage channel B so that it no longer matches the other channels
Wrong reference value from another high-voltage unit (rear motor unit, battery management)

P0E8E.d: P0E8E means the output of inverter voltage sensor B for drive motor A has fallen to the bottom end of its scale. On the 2023 Outlander PHEV Mitsubishi assigns it to the main measuring channel of capacitor 2 (V2M) in the power drive unit and sets it when that signal stays at no more than 0.45 V for 0.16 s, provided the unit has at least 8 V supply; monitoring runs continuously.
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Vehicle not ready to drive or only engine power available
c: Measuring circuit for capacitor 2 inside the power drive unit failed
Signal line shorted to ground or open
No high voltage on the bus because of a blown fuse or open contactor path

P0E8F.d: P0E8F is the upper-limit fault of inverter voltage sensor B on drive motor A. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV sets it when the main channel at capacitor 2 (V2M) reports at least 4.75 V for 0.16 s, again with the unit supplied at 8 V or above, and lists it as a range check maximum.
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Electric drive switched off or strongly reduced
c: Measuring circuit for capacitor 2 inside the power drive unit defective
Signal shorted to sensor supply or lost sensor ground
Actual overvoltage on the high-voltage bus
