P0E90.d: P0E90 is meant for a voltage sensor B signal of the drive motor A inverter that flickers, jumps or drops out for moments without staying wrong long enough for the low or high code. No manufacturer documents P0E90 publicly.
s: Hybrid warning that comes and goes
Short power interruptions or jerky electric drive
c: Loose or corroded low-voltage connector on the inverter
Chafed or partly broken signal lead
Measuring circuit in the power electronics failing intermittently with heat or vibration

P0E91.d: P0E91 is the circuit code for the second DC voltage channel, sensor B, in the inverter of drive motor B, usually the second electric machine or the rear axle motor. It applies when this signal is absent or electrically unusable without a more precise verdict; its partner channel A is coded P0DA3, and the matching code for drive motor A is P0E8C.
s: Hybrid or EV warning with MIL
Loss of the second drive motor (for example no all-wheel drive), reduced power
c: Voltage channel B measuring circuit in the motor B inverter defective
Connector or harness of the motor B inverter loose or damaged
Software fault in the motor B control unit

P0E92.d: P0E92 is stored when voltage sensor B of the drive motor B inverter gives a reading inside its electrical range that does not fit the other voltage values of the high-voltage system. No manufacturer documents P0E92 publicly.
s: MIL and hybrid or EV system warning
Second drive motor switched off, reduced acceleration
c: Voltage channel B of the motor B inverter drifts
Internal fault of the motor B inverter or motor unit
Wrong comparison value from battery management or the front power electronics

P0E93.d: With P0E93 the controller sees the B voltage channel in the motor B inverter stuck near the bottom of its signal range, as happens with a short to ground, an open signal path or a failed measuring circuit. No manufacturer documents P0E93 publicly.
s: MIL and EV system warning
Rear or second motor without power, front-drive only
c: Measuring circuit for channel B in the motor B inverter failed
Signal line shorted to ground or open
High-voltage cable or connection to motor B open, no voltage at the inverter

P0E94.d: P0E94 records that voltage sensor B in the drive motor B inverter reports a value at the top of its signal range. A short from the signal to a supply, an interrupted sensor ground or a defective measuring stage are the usual explanations; a genuine overvoltage would normally show on the other channels too.
s: MIL and EV system warning
Second drive motor deactivated, less traction and power
c: Measuring stage for channel B in the motor B inverter defective
Signal shorted to a supply or lost sensor ground
Real overvoltage on the high-voltage bus

P0E95.d: P0E95 closes the sensor B series for drive motor B: the signal is unstable, with brief dropouts or spikes, rather than permanently low, high or implausible. No manufacturer documents P0E95 publicly.
s: EV or hybrid warning that appears and clears again
Second motor drops out briefly, uneven traction
c: Corroded or loose connector on the motor B inverter
Harness damaged where it moves with the axle or suspension
Measuring circuit in the motor B inverter failing intermittently

P0E96.d: P0E96 opens the series for a third voltage measurement in a DC/DC converter, sensor C. It is the general circuit code, meant for a missing or electrically invalid signal; range, low, high and erratic faults of the same sensor follow from P0E97 to P0E9A.
s: 12 V or converter warning, possibly with MIL
Start-stop or 12 V support restricted
c: Measuring circuit for channel C inside the converter defective
Loose connector or damaged sensing lead
Software fault in the converter or its controller

P0E97.d: P0E97 is the plausibility code for the third voltage channel of a DC/DC converter: sensor C delivers an electrically valid value that does not agree with what the controller expects. Two makers document it.
s: MIL on, often without a noticeable driving fault
12 V battery or high-voltage warning messages in the cluster
Fault entry appears sporadically and returns after clearing
c: Converter or power electronics software with too tight plausibility limits
Converter stuck in an error state after an incorrect wake-up
Drifting voltage measurement inside the converter

P0E98.d: P0E98 is set when the C voltage channel of a DC/DC converter is stuck at the lowest end of its range, typically because the measuring line is grounded or the sensing stage has lost its supply. No manufacturer documents P0E98 publicly.
s: MIL on, depending on the manufacturer's rating
Converter output reduced or switched to a fallback value
Start-stop or 12 V support may be disabled
c: Sensor C signal line shorted to ground
Measuring stage without supply or with an open signal path
Internal defect in the converter's measuring circuit

P0E99.d: With P0E99 the controller finds the voltage sensor C reading of a DC/DC converter pinned near its upper limit. That points to the signal touching a battery feed or reference supply, or to a broken sensor ground that lets the input float up, rather than to a real converter overvoltage.
s: MIL and charging or 12 V warning possible
Converter limits or stops its output
Start-stop function unavailable
c: Sensor C signal shorted to battery voltage or reference supply
Open sensor ground letting the signal float high
Actual overvoltage from a faulty converter regulation

P0E9A.d: P0E9A completes the sensor C voltage series of a DC/DC converter. It is meant for a signal that jumps, flickers or drops out for brief moments, which the low and high tests miss because they need a fault to persist.
s: Warning lamp that appears and disappears
Short interruptions of start-stop or 12 V support
Code often stored as history only
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the sensor C path
Harness chafing intermittently at a moving point
Cracked solder joint in the converter's measuring circuit

P0E9B.d: P0E9B opens the series for the second current measurement of a DC/DC converter, sensor B. It covers a signal that is absent or unusable on the electrical level and that the controller cannot classify as low, high or implausible; those cases follow as P0E9C to P0E9F.
s: High-voltage or 12 V system warning
Converter output reduced, 12 V battery charged less
Possibly reduced drive power
c: Fault in the converter's internal current sensing
Connector or wiring fault on the sensor B path

P0E9C.d: P0E9C means current sensor B of a DC/DC converter gives a value within its electrical window that does not match the operating state, for example a current that stays put while the load changes, or that differs from the figure the controller derives from voltages and switching. No manufacturer documents P0E9C publicly.
s: MIL, sometimes after a single trip
Reduced converter output and weak 12 V charging
Power reduction warning possible
c: Current sensor B drifting or with a shifted zero point
Fault in the converter power stage causing unexpected currents
Software with an unsuitable plausibility window

P0E9D.d: P0E9D reports that the signal of DC/DC converter current sensor B has dropped below its valid range. Porsche documents it for the Taycan of model years 2020 to 2024 as P0E9D00, current sensor 2 of the converter with a short to ground, logged by the HV power electronics on the front axle (A49), the rear axle (A50) or both.
s: Red warning to stop the vehicle safely
Fault no longer active after an ignition cycle
Drive power reduced or vehicle not ready to drive
c: Current monitoring threshold set too low in the software
Sensor B signal shorted to ground
Sensor supply missing inside the power electronics

P0E9E.d: P0E9E flags the B current channel of a DC/DC converter reading above its ceiling: the raw signal lies above anything the sensor should output. With a Hall sensor whose zero lies mid-scale, this usually means the signal line touches the supply or the reference ground has opened.
s: Red 12 V battery or HV warning
Converter stops supplying the 12 V network
Reduced drive power possible
c: Sensor B signal shorted to supply voltage
Open reference ground of the current sensor
Converter in an error state after wake-up, cleared by reset

P0E9F.d: P0E9F is reserved for a current sensor B signal of a DC/DC converter that is unsteady: it spikes, drops out or shows noise yet never stays out of bounds for long. Publicly, no maker describes P0E9F.
s: Warnings that come and go
Brief converter derating
Code stored without a current fault
c: Loose terminal or connector on the sensor B path
Solder joint that opens under heat or vibration
Electrical interference on the measuring line

P0EA0.d: P0EA0 covers circuit faults of a third current channel inside a DC/DC converter, sensor C. Converters with several phases or with separate input and output sensing can carry more than two current channels; the letter C simply names the third.
s: Warning for the high-voltage or 12 V system
Converter limited to a reduced output
MIL depending on the manufacturer
c: Defect in the converter's third current sensing channel
Damaged connector or wiring on the sensor C path
Software fault in the signal evaluation

P0EA1.d: P0EA1 stands for a sensor C current reading that is electrically plausible yet disagrees with the converter's operating point or with its sister channels. If a converter measures several phase currents, those values should track each other, and one channel that deviates is a typical trigger.
s: MIL, possibly after one trip
Reduced 12 V charging current
Converter or drive power derated
c: Sensor C channel drifting away from the other channels
Fault in the converter phase measured by sensor C
Plausibility software in need of an update

P0EA2.d: P0EA2 is stored when current sensor C of a DC/DC converter reports a raw value under its lower limit. Because current sensors in these units normally place their zero-current output at mid-supply, a value near zero volts rarely means low current; it points to a ground short, a lost sensor supply or a broken signal path.
s: Warning lamp and possibly a stop request
Converter switched off or derated
12 V battery discharges while driving
c: Sensor C signal shorted to ground
Missing supply voltage of the current sensor
Monitoring threshold in the software set too tight

P0EA3.d: P0EA3 marks a current sensor C signal above the top of its accepted window. Electrically this means the signal line touching a voltage source, an open sensor ground or a failed output stage of the sensor; a genuine overcurrent of the converter is a different matter and has its own code, P0D33.
s: 12 V or high-voltage warning in the cluster
Converter output stopped
Reduced performance possible
c: Sensor C signal shorted to supply
Open ground of the current sensor

P0EA4.d: P0EA4 ends the current sensor C series and describes a signal that wavers or breaks off momentarily instead of failing steadily. No manufacturer documents P0EA4 publicly.
s: Sporadic warnings without a lasting fault
12 V battery not kept fully charged
Start-stop occasionally disabled
c: Outdated control software evaluating the signal too strictly
Loose plug or damaged pin on the sensor C path
Connection that opens with temperature changes

P0EA5.d: P0EA5 says that a second DC/DC converter, B, does not deliver what it is asked to, for example the commanded output voltage or current, although its sensors give no circuit fault. FCA documents it as DC/DC Converter 2 Performance for the 2019 Jeep Cherokee (KL) with the 3.2 litre V6 and engine start/stop: PCM flash bulletins 18-023-19 REV.
s: MIL on
Engine does not restart after an auto-stop, start-stop disabled
Voltage dips in the 12 V network, for example audio dropouts
c: Engine or powertrain control software needing an update
Poor supply or ground connection of converter B

P0EA6.d: P0EA6 means the second DC/DC converter, B, has reached a temperature beyond its permitted limit. Unlike a temperature sensor code, the reading itself is accepted as true; the unit is simply too hot and will normally reduce or stop its output to protect itself.
s: MIL on
Start-stop unavailable while the converter is hot
Electrical consumers affected during engine restart
c: Cooling air or heat sink of converter B obstructed
Sustained high load on the 12 V network
Control software misjudging the temperature condition
Weak internal power stage of converter B

P0EA7.d: P0EA7 reports that an auxiliary cooling loop, a coolant circuit kept apart from the main engine circuit, does not achieve the cooling effect the controller expects. Volvo documents the code for its T8 plug-in hybrids of model years 2016 to 2019 (XC90, S90, XC60, S60 and others): the engine control module stores P0EA773, fault type actuator stuck closed, and turns on the check-engine light.
s: Check-engine light on
Often no noticeable change in driving behaviour
Possible power limits on electric drive parts that run too warm
c: Thermostat in the auxiliary loop sticking closed (Volvo T8, earlier part design)
Low coolant level or trapped air in the auxiliary loop
Weak or failed auxiliary coolant pump
Module software reporting the fault wrongly (Ford Mustang GTD)

P0EA8.d: P0EA8 is the general circuit code for the second high-voltage measurement of an electric A/C compressor, labelled sensor B. Such compressors draw their power from the traction battery and convert it in a built-in inverter; the module reads the supply voltage to control the motor and protect its power stage.
s: Air conditioning does not cool
Fault message for the climate system
Battery cooling via refrigerant may be unavailable during charging
c: Interrupted voltage sense path inside or at the compressor
Fault on the compressor's inverter or control board
Poorly seated high-voltage or signal connector at the compressor

P0EA9.d: P0EA9 means the B voltage reading reported by the electric A/C compressor looks electrically valid but does not fit other information, usually the high voltage reported by the battery system that feeds the compressor directly. No manufacturer documents P0EA9 publicly.
s: Air conditioning switches off or works only now and then
Fault often recorded without any other symptom
c: Drifting voltage measurement inside the compressor module
Faulty data exchange between compressor and hybrid controller
Wrong battery voltage reference from the hybrid or battery controller

P0EAA.d: P0EAA flags a B voltage reading at the top of, or beyond, the plausible range of the compressor supply. Since the battery cannot really deliver that much, the cause usually lies in the measurement itself: an open or shorted sense path, a failed voltage divider inside the compressor or a wrong reference.
s: Compressor stops, cabin is not cooled
Warning in the climate control display
c: Failed voltage divider or reference in the compressor module
Sense line shorted to a higher potential
Actual overvoltage on the high-voltage bus

P0EAB.d: P0EAB is set when the B voltage channel of the electric A/C compressor reports far less than the high-voltage battery actually supplies while the contactors are closed. Typical reasons are a sense line shorted to ground, a broken internal connection or a sensing stage without supply; a supply interrupted upstream, for instance by a high-voltage fuse, produces the same picture and should be ruled out first.
s: No cooling from the air conditioning
Charging power may be reduced if the battery cannot be cooled
c: Voltage sense line shorted to ground
High-voltage supply to the compressor interrupted (fuse, connector)
Measuring stage in the compressor module without supply

P0EAC.d: P0EAC points to a B voltage signal that jumps or drops out for short moments instead of staying wrong. The module sees sudden changes no real battery voltage can make, or values that come and go.
s: Air conditioning cuts out briefly and then resumes
Fault entry returns after clearing
c: Loose or corroded connector at the compressor
Harness chafed or cracked by engine and road vibration
Cracked solder joint on the compressor control board

P0EAD.d: P0EAD covers the current sensor of an electric A/C compressor, which measures how much current the motor drive takes from the high-voltage link. The controller needs this value to limit power and to shield the power stage and the high-voltage pack from overload.
s: Compressor does not start, no cooling
Fault stored in the climate or compressor module
c: Failed current sensing element in the compressor power module
Open internal connection between sensor and control board
Compressor or climate module software error

P0EAE.d: P0EAE says the compressor current reading is electrically valid but does not fit the operating state, for example a value that does not match motor speed or load. Audi documents the code for the 2016 A3 e-tron: P0EAE00 is stored as a passive or sporadic entry in the Climatronic module J255, the MIL is lit at the request of another module over the vehicle network while the engine module holds no code, and P26FD00 may
s: MIL on without an engine module fault code
Air conditioning may or may not be restricted
Entry stored as passive or sporadic
c: Calculation error in the climate module software (Audi A3 e-tron, update available)
Drifting current measurement in the compressor
Internal compressor fault confirmed by the guided test

P0EAF.d: P0EAF reports that the compressor current signal sits at the bottom of its measuring range. In a running compressor this cannot be true, so the module suspects the measuring chain: a grounded signal path, a sensing chip without supply or an offset error inside the power module.
s: Compressor shut down, warm air from the vents
Climate system fault message
c: Current signal path shorted to ground
Offset error of the measurement in the power module

P0EB0.d: P0EB0 flags a current sensor signal at the top end of its range, beyond what the compressor drive could ever draw. It differs from a genuine overcurrent such as P0D6F, where the measurement is trusted and the motor is overloaded: here the signal itself is suspect, for example after a short to a supply voltage or a failed sensing element.
s: Compressor switches off right after starting
No cooling, fault message in the climate display
c: Current signal shorted to a supply voltage
Failed sensing element in the compressor inverter
Real overload from a stiff compressor or excessive refrigerant charge

P0EB1.d: Electric A/C compressors run a three-phase permanent-magnet motor whose inverter measures the phase currents in order to commutate it and limit torque. P0EB1 is the general circuit fault of the phase U current sensor: the controller gets no usable signal and gives no finer verdict on it.
s: Compressor does not run, cabin stays warm
Climate system warning
c: Failed phase U current sensor in the compressor inverter
Open signal path between sensor and inverter controller
Fault on the inverter control board

P0EB2.d: P0EB2 is set when the phase U current sensor of the electric A/C compressor sends a signal above its valid window. Current sensors in such inverters often output a voltage centred on zero current, so a stuck-high output reads like a large current in one direction even with the motor at rest.
s: Compressor will not start or stops at once
No cooling during hot weather
c: Phase U signal shorted to the sensor supply
Damaged Hall element of the phase U sensor
Defect on the inverter board affecting the U channel

P0EB3.d: P0EB3 means the phase U current signal has fallen below its permitted range. Depending on the sensor design this looks like a large negative current or like no signal at all; either way the controller can no longer trust the U-phase value it needs to drive the motor smoothly.
s: Air conditioning inoperative
Fault message after switching the A/C on
c: Phase U sensing path shorted to ground
Supply to the phase U sensor missing
Internal fault in the compressor inverter

P0EB4.d: P0EB4 concerns the plausibility of the phase U current reading of an electric A/C compressor. The value is in range but disagrees with what the controller can work out for itself: in a motor fed by three wires the phase currents must add up to roughly zero, and each phase should follow the commanded current pattern.
s: Compressor runs roughly or noisily before switching off
Reduced or intermittent cooling
c: Offset or gain drift of the phase U sensor
Ageing measurement circuit on the inverter board
Winding fault in the compressor motor distorting the currents

P0EB5.d: P0EB5 is the high-range fault of the phase V current sensor in the compressor inverter. The reading lies above the window the sensor can produce in normal service, which points to a short towards supply voltage, a defective sensing element or an internal fault in the power module rather than to real overcurrent.
s: Compressor switched off, no cooling
Battery may warm up more during fast charging
c: Phase V signal shorted towards supply voltage
Internal fault in the compressor power module

P0EB6.d: P0EB6 reports that the phase V current signal reads below its permissible minimum. The compressor's power module cannot regulate phase V without it and stops the motor.
s: No air conditioning
Fault stored in the compressor control module
c: Phase V sensing path pulled to ground
Phase V sensor has lost its supply
Defect in the V channel of the inverter board

P0EB7.d: With P0EB7 the compressor's phase V current value passes the electrical limits but is not credible. The controller compares it with the other two phases and with the current it is commanding; a persistent offset, a reading that lags or is scaled wrongly, or a three-phase sum far from zero all point at the V sensor.
s: Uneven compressor running or humming noise
Cooling weakens, then fails
c: Persistent offset or scaling error of the phase V sensor
Slow or filtered V-phase measurement on the inverter board
Fault in the V winding or its internal lead

P0EB8.d: P0EB8 indicates that the phase W current sensor of the compressor inverter delivers a value above its usable range. Since the motor is not actually drawing such a current, a short to a positive supply in the sensing circuit or a failed sensor element is the most probable explanation.
s: A/C stops working, warning shown
Compressor will not restart until the fault is cleared
c: W-phase sensing circuit shorted to a positive supply
Fault in the W input of the inverter controller

P0EB9.d: P0EB9 is stored when the phase W current signal drops beneath its lower limit, for instance after the signal wire has made contact with ground or after the sensor has lost its feed. The value is then useless for motor control, and the compressor module shuts the drive down rather than run it on two phases of information.
s: No cooling, compressor silent
Climate fault indicated
c: Phase W measuring line shorted to ground
Defect of the W measurement inside the compressor module

P0EBA.d: P0EBA covers an implausible phase W current reading in an electric A/C compressor: the signal stays in range, yet it does not agree with the commanded current, the rotor position or the two other phases. No manufacturer documents P0EBA publicly.
s: Compressor runs unevenly, then stops
Cooling capacity drops
c: Fault in the W measurement on the inverter board
Rotor position estimate disturbed, making the W current look wrong

P0EBB.d: P0EBB is the general circuit code for the compressor's phase V current sensor, numbered after the W-phase codes instead of at the start of the V series. The module receives no usable V-phase value at all and does not classify it further as high, low or implausible.
s: Compressor does not run
Air conditioning and possibly battery cooling unavailable
c: Loose internal plug between sensor and board
Failed phase V sensor or inverter board

P0EBC.d: P0EBC is the general circuit fault of the first refrigerant temperature sensor in the air conditioning loop: the control module gets no usable reading from it and does not narrow the fault down to high or low. Volkswagen lists P0EBC00 for the 2021 ID.4 as an electrical fault of refrigerant temperature sensor 1 in the A/C module (address 0008).
s: Air conditioning inoperative or not cooling
Fault entry stored in the climate control module
c: Internal electrical fault of the refrigerant pressure/temperature sender (VW G395)
Corroded connector or damaged wiring to the sensor
Faulty sensor input in the climate control module

P0EBD.d: P0EBD means the signal voltage of refrigerant temperature sensor A sits at the top of its range. With the usual NTC thermistor that equals an extremely cold reading, and in practice it points to an open signal path, a disconnected plug or a short to the reference voltage.
s: Compressor stays off or A/C output is reduced
Implausibly low refrigerant temperature in live data
c: Open signal or ground wire, or unplugged connector
Signal wire shorted to the reference or supply voltage

P0EBE.d: P0EBE is logged when the voltage from refrigerant temperature sensor A falls close to zero. For an NTC element a low voltage stands for high temperature, so the controller sees refrigerant that seems far too hot.
s: A/C compressor switched off as a precaution
Live data shows an unrealistically hot refrigerant
c: Signal wire chafed and shorted to ground

P0EBF.d: P0EBF reports that sensor A gives an electrically valid but implausible refrigerant temperature. Three makers name it.
s: Check engine lamp on (Volvo) or MIL requested by the climate module (Audi)
Fault stored as intermittent or sporadic
A/C may cool poorly or not at all
c: Software misjudgement after preconditioning or self-check (Volvo, Audi; update available)
Wrong refrigerant charge distorting the comparison values

P0EC0.d: P0EC0 is the umbrella circuit code for the phase W current sensor in the inverter of an electric A/C compressor. It applies when no valid W-phase value arrives at all, without a split into high, low or implausible; those cases have their own codes P0EB8 to P0EBA.
s: Electric A/C compressor does not start
No cabin cooling, battery cooling via refrigerant may be limited
c: Interrupted W-phase sensing path inside the inverter
Failed W-phase current sensor or inverter board
Missing supply voltage for the current sensors

P0EC1.d: P0EC1 covers a circuit fault of a second refrigerant temperature sensor, found mainly on electrified cars whose heat pump or battery chiller measures the refrigerant at several points. The module receives no usable value from sensor B.
s: Heat pump or A/C switched off or limited
Fault stored in the climate control module
c: Failed sensor B or combined pressure/temperature sender
Wiring, connector or shared LIN line fault
Mixed part versions on one LIN line after a repair

P0EC2.d: With P0EC2 the signal of refrigerant temperature sensor B is stuck near the reference voltage. An NTC thermistor would only get there at extreme cold, so an open circuit somewhere in the loop is far more likely.
s: Very low refrigerant temperature shown for sensor B
Heating via heat pump or cooling unavailable
c: Open signal or ground line between sensor B and module
Connector not fully seated after A/C work

P0EC3.d: P0EC3 stands for a sensor B signal pulled down toward ground. Because a thermistor of the NTC type lowers its resistance as it warms, the module reads a refrigerant temperature far above anything the system could reach.
s: A/C compressor held off, cabin not cooled
Charging or driving power possibly limited if battery cooling depends on the loop
c: Harness pinched against the body, signal shorted to ground
Water ingress in the sensor plug

P0EC4.d: P0EC4 is a plausibility fault: sensor B delivers a voltage inside its normal window, yet the temperature it reports does not agree with other information. No manufacturer documents P0EC4 publicly.
s: Uneven or weak cooling, compressor cycling oddly
Fault often appears only after a long standstill
c: Sensor B drifting out of tolerance
Sensor not seated properly on the pipe, poor thermal contact
Incorrect refrigerant charge shifting the comparison values

P0EC5.d: P0EC5 means the speed information of the electrically driven compressor motor is implausible: the motor does not turn at the speed the controller expects, or the reported value contradicts other data. Mazda uses the code on the 2024 to 2026 CX-90 PHEV and 2025 to 2026 CX-70 PHEV, describing P0EC5:00 in the PCM as an error signal coming from the compressor.
s: A/C does not cool
Accompanying compressor voltage, communication or insulation codes
c: Internal short in the electric compressor after overcurrent (Mazda PHEV)
Blown high-voltage A/C fuse cutting compressor power
Mechanical drag or lack of oil keeping the motor below target speed

P0EC6.d: P0EC6 concerns the control side of the relay that switches power to air conditioning components, typically the compressor or climate electronics. The module driving the relay coil notices that its output does not behave as commanded, most often because the coil circuit is open.
s: A/C or electric compressor completely without function
No relay click when A/C is requested
c: Relay coil burnt open or relay missing
Open control wire or loose relay socket terminal
Failed output driver in the controlling module

P0EC7.d: P0EC7 is set when the control line of the relay feeding the A/C reads too low a voltage, usually because it is shorted to ground. What the driver feels depends on how the coil is switched: with a low-side driver a grounded line can keep the relay energised even with the A/C off, while with a high-side driver the relay simply cannot be switched on.
s: A/C power stays on with A/C switched off, or never switches on
Possible battery drain while parked if the relay stays energised
c: Relay control line chafed and shorted to ground
Shorted turns in the relay coil
Output stage of the module stuck low

P0EC8.d: P0EC8 indicates that the relay control circuit for the A/C power supply carries too high a voltage, typically a short to a battery-fed wire. A low-side driver then pushes current straight into that short when it switches on; modern output stages detect the overcurrent, turn themselves off and log this code, so the relay stays open and the A/C components get no power.
s: A/C has no power and stays off
Relay may stay energised permanently on high-side switched designs
c: Control line shorted to a battery-fed wire
Relay coil with too low resistance overloading the driver

P0EC9.d: P0EC9 reports that refrigerant distribution valve A, a solenoid valve that splits refrigerant between branches of the A/C circuit, stays open or does not close on command. Such a fault is usually detected indirectly, because pressure or temperature behind the valve fails to react when it should be shut.
s: MIL on without a code in the engine control module
Code stored passive/sporadic in the climate control module
Reduced or uneven cooling in one branch, or no noticeable change at all
c: Faulty self-test calculation in the climate control software (Audi A3 e-tron, fixed by update)
Valve held open by dirt, debris or a sticking armature
Weak solenoid coil that no longer pulls the valve fully shut

P0ECA.d: P0ECA treats the temperature sensors of the hybrid or traction battery as one system: the battery controller compares the readings with each other and flags the group when one of them strays from the rest or shows an impossible value. Ford documents it for its 2019 hybrid and plug-in models.
s: Hybrid or battery warning, MIL depending on manufacturer
Reduced electric power or charging rate
On the Bentayga, Dynamic Ride fault message and no roll compensation
c: One battery thermistor drifting away from the others
Battery controller software misjudging the comparison (Bentley super capacitor, update 114)
Loose or corroded connector on the temperature sense harness inside the pack
Genuine local hot spot, e.g. a blocked cooling channel at one module

P0ECB.d: P0ECB indicates that the voltage measurements of the hybrid/EV battery contradict each other. Battery controllers usually capture the same voltage along more than one path, for example the whole pack directly and as the sum of all cell readings, or each half of the pack against its own cells; once these paths drift apart, at least one sensor must be wrong.
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Limited electric power, unstable state of charge display
Contactors may stay open, vehicle may not reach ready mode
c: Drifting pack or half-pack voltage sensor in the battery controller
Loose or corroded cell sense lead falsifying the cell sum
Internal fault of the cell monitoring electronics
Measurement taken on the wrong side of a contactor that is not fully closed

P0ECC.d: P0ECC is the general voltage code for hybrid/EV battery E. The letters A to F mark separately monitored sub-batteries, modules or energy stores of one system; E is the fifth, so the code can only occur where a manufacturer divides its storage into at least five such units.
s: Battery or hybrid warning, MIL
Reduced electric power and range
c: Aged or damaged cells in unit E
Fault in the voltage sense leads or connectors of unit E
Battery controller measuring or software fault

P0ECD.d: P0ECD flags an unstable voltage in hybrid/EV battery E: the value moves faster or further than the controller tolerates, whereas a lasting offset would set P0ECE or P0ECF. No manufacturer documents P0ECD publicly.
s: Intermittent battery warning, often only under load
Power drops during acceleration
MIL on
c: Cell with high internal resistance whose voltage collapses under load
Loose busbar screw or cell connector in unit E
Corroded or intermittent voltage sense terminal
Battery controller software, curable by update

P0ECE.d: P0ECE sets when the voltage of hybrid/EV battery E remains below the window the controller expects for the present load and charge. Its counterparts are P0ECF for too high and P0ECD for unstable readings.
s: Reduced electric range and acceleration
Engine starts more often, EV mode unavailable
MIL and battery warning
c: Unit E deeply discharged after long standstill or a high self-discharge cell
Internal short or capacity loss in a module of unit E
Balancing switch stuck on and draining one cell group

P0ECF.d: P0ECF is stored when unit E of the hybrid/EV battery exceeds its upper voltage limit. It mirrors P0ECE, while unstable readings belong to P0ECD.
s: Charging or regenerative braking blocked
Battery warning, MIL
Vehicle may switch off the high-voltage system
c: Cell balancing of unit E no longer works, group overcharged
Voltage sense channel reading too high

P0ED0.d: P0ED0 is the general voltage code of hybrid/EV battery F, the sixth and last unit in this letter series. It reports an implausible voltage of the unit without separating unstable (P0ED1), low (P0ED2) and high (P0ED3) readings.
s: MIL and battery warning
Reduced electric power
c: Aged or damaged cells in unit F
Open or high-resistance voltage sense lead of unit F
Cell monitoring electronics or software fault

P0ED1.d: P0ED1 reports that the voltage of hybrid/EV battery F fluctuates beyond the permitted band instead of staying steadily off, which would be P0ED2 or P0ED3. No manufacturer documents P0ED1 publicly.
s: Warning that comes and goes, often over bumps or under load
Short power reductions while driving
MIL on
c: Cell group of unit F drifting because balancing cannot keep up
Sense lead or connector with intermittent contact

P0ED2.d: P0ED2 means hybrid/EV battery F delivers less voltage than the controller predicts from current draw and state of charge. No manufacturer documents P0ED2 publicly.
s: Less power in electric mode
Shorter electric range
MIL and battery warning
c: Aged module in unit F with lost capacity
Cell with internal leakage drained during standstill
High-resistance connection inside unit F dropping voltage under load

P0ED3.d: P0ED3 is logged once battery F of the hybrid/EV system climbs above its permitted maximum voltage. It is the high member of the F series, next to P0ED2 (low) and P0ED1 (unstable).
s: Charging refused or regenerative braking weak
MIL and battery warning
c: Balancing circuit of unit F failed, cells overcharged
Measuring channel of unit F reading too high

P0ED4.d: P0ED4 is the general current fault for phase X of the hybrid generator. J2012 names the generator phases U, V and W and adds a separate X, Y, Z series, which presumably serves machines with a second three-phase winding set fed by its own inverter bridge; which vehicles use it is not published, and no manufacturer documents P0ED4.
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Reduced charging, engine may start less smoothly
c: Fault in the inverter bridge or current regulation for phase X
Phase X current sensor out of tolerance
Loose or damaged high-voltage connection of phase X

P0ED5.d: P0ED5 means that phase X of the hybrid generator carries, or appears to carry, too little current while the generator is supposed to deliver torque. No manufacturer documents P0ED5 publicly.
s: Weak or no battery charging by the generator
Rough engine start or vibration from the generator
MIL and hybrid warning
c: Open or loose phase X cable or terminal
Inverter power switch for phase X not conducting
Burnt or broken winding connection in the generator

P0ED6.d: P0ED6 is stored when the current in phase X of the hybrid generator exceeds its permitted limit. No manufacturer documents P0ED6 publicly.
s: Sudden hybrid system shutdown or loss of ready mode
MIL and hybrid warning
c: Turn-to-turn or ground short in the phase X winding
Current sensor reading too high (false overcurrent)

P0ED7.d: P0ED7 is the general current code for phase Y, the middle phase of the generator's X-Y-Z set. Without being narrowed to low (P0ED8) or high (P0ED9), it says that the Y current no longer behaves as the inverter controller expects.
s: Hybrid warning and MIL
Limited generator operation
c: Inverter fault affecting the phase Y bridge
Phase cables mixed up or poorly seated after repair work

P0ED8.d: P0ED8 reports too little current in phase Y of the hybrid generator. No manufacturer documents P0ED8 publicly.
s: Generator delivers less charging power
Uneven running or noise from the transaxle
MIL and hybrid warning
c: Open or corroded phase Y cable or terminal
Inverter switch for phase Y not turning on
Phase Y current sensor reading too low

P0ED9.d: P0ED9 is set when phase Y of the hybrid generator draws more current than allowed. No manufacturer documents P0ED9 publicly.
s: Hybrid system shuts down, vehicle may lose ready mode
MIL and hybrid warning
c: Short in the phase Y winding or to the housing
Chafed phase cable shorting to ground

P0EDA.d: P0EDA is the general current fault of phase Z, the last of the three X-Y-Z generator phases, without the detail of P0EDB (low) or P0EDC (high). No manufacturer documents P0EDA publicly.
s: Hybrid warning, often with further phase or sum codes
Reduced charging and generator assist
c: Phase Z current sensor offset or failure
Inverter fault on the phase Z bridge
Poor contact at the phase Z high-voltage terminal

P0EDB.d: P0EDB means phase Z of the hybrid generator shows less current than the commanded operating point calls for. No manufacturer documents P0EDB publicly.
s: Humming or vibration from the hybrid transaxle
Reduced generator power and charging
MIL and hybrid warning
c: Loose or corroded phase Z high-voltage terminal
Broken conductor in the phase Z winding
Power switch for phase Z no longer conducting

P0EDC.d: P0EDC is the overcurrent code for phase Z of the hybrid generator and ends the X-Y-Z series. No manufacturer documents P0EDC publicly; the closest published logic is Ford's for its U-V-W generator phases (P0A71, P0A74, P0A77), which also flags any current above 15 A in the first 200 ms after power-up, a moment when the machine should be idle.
s: Hybrid system shutdown, engine may not start
MIL and hybrid warning, possibly with sum check codes
c: Damaged or leaking power module for phase Z
Insulation fault or turn short in the phase Z winding

P0EDD.d: P0EDD is the state-of-health verdict for the second section of a traction battery: section B has lost so much capacity or gained so much internal resistance that it falls below the maker's limit. P0A7F covers section A, P0EDE to P0EE1 sections C to F.
s: MIL or hybrid system warning on
Noticeably shorter electric range
Engine runs more often, less electric assist
c: Battery module or cell group in section B aged beyond its limit
Battery controller software misjudging state of health (FCA reflash cases)
Pack defect covered by a warranty extension (Pacifica Hybrid)

P0EDE.d: P0EDE flags the third battery section, C, as worn out. The controller estimates each section's usable capacity and resistance from voltage behaviour under load and at rest; if section C drifts too far from its new-state values, it is judged deteriorated.
s: Check engine lamp on
Displayed electric range too low
Electric driving mode cannot be selected or ends early
c: Cells in battery group 3 aged (capacity loss, higher resistance)
Strong voltage spread inside the section
Controller estimate wrong, module still healthy

P0EDF.d: P0EDF belongs to the fourth section of the traction battery. It is not a sensor or wiring code but a capacity and power judgement: the battery controller has concluded that section D can no longer deliver what the maker expects of a healthy unit.
s: MIL on
Reduced electric range and power
c: High-voltage module of group 4 worn out
Single weak cell pulling the section down
Evaluation logic of the battery controller

P0EE0.d: With P0EE0 the controller reports ageing of section E, the fifth part of the traction battery. A section is usually a module or a group of cell blocks with its own monitoring; once its share of the pack has lost too much capacity or become too resistive, the whole battery can no longer reach its rated energy, which shows up first as shorter electric range.
s: Electric range shown too low
Engine warning lamp on
Less power in electric mode
c: Cell voltages in the section spread too far (often with P0BBD)

P0EE1.d: P0EE1 is the last code of the P0E range for section ageing and covers section F. The series runs A (P0A7F) and B to F (P0EDD to P0EE1); for further sections J2012 continues in the P2 block, with G and H as P2CCC and P2CCD.
s: MIL on
Shorter electric range
c: Section aged faster due to heat or poor cooling
Evaluation error of the battery controller

P0EE2.d: P0EE2 says the second refrigerant distribution valve, B, stays open or fails to close. In plug-in hybrids and EVs such shut-off valves route refrigerant either to the cabin evaporator or to a chiller that cools the battery; Egelhof sells solenoid versions with 12 V or 24 V coils for exactly this use.
s: MIL on
Weaker cabin or battery cooling
Often no noticeable effect beyond the warning
c: Thermal management software misjudging the valve (Audi J1024)
Valve seat contaminated or armature stuck open
Weak coil that no longer moves the armature

P0EE3.d: P0EE3 concerns the wiring between the controlling module and refrigerant valve B, most often an interrupted path. With the output switched off, the driver normally sees a defined voltage through the coil; with it switched on, current flows.
s: Warning lamp on
Valve B no longer switches, affected refrigerant branch stays as it is
c: Loose, corroded or pushed-back pin at the valve connector
Broken coil winding in valve B
Broken wire in the harness to the valve

P0EE4.d: P0EE4 is stored when the control line of refrigerant valve B is pulled to a lower voltage than the driver commands, usually by a short to ground. With a high-side driver the valve would then stay energised or the output would be overloaded; with a low-side driver the coil may be switched on permanently.
s: Warning lamp on
Valve B behaves as if permanently energised or not at all
c: Control wire chafed through to ground
Coil winding shorted to the valve body

P0EE5.d: P0EE5 means the control line of refrigerant valve B carries more voltage than its commanded state allows. If the driver switches the coil to ground, a short to a 12 V feed is the classic reason; with some driver types an open coil can also float the line high.
s: Warning lamp on
Cabin or battery cooling not working as requested
c: Control wire shorted to a 12 V feed
Open coil letting the line float high
Faulty output stage in the controlling module

P0EE6.d: P0EE6 is reported by the output stage itself: the switch that powers refrigerant valve B has measured too much current or got too hot and has protected itself. Modern smart high-side switches do this on chip; TI's TPS1HB16-Q1, for example, has an adjustable current limit between 4.4 and 49 A, shuts down at about 150 C junction temperature with roughly 20 C hysteresis, and flags the event on its diagnostic output.
s: Warning lamp on
Valve B switched off, cooling branch not served
c: Shorted turns in the valve B coil raising the current
Partial short in the valve wiring

P0EE7.d: P0EE7 is the general circuit code for the second temperature sensor of the charging inlet. High-current inlets carry several sensors; the supplier Sailtran fits one PT1000 at the L1 pin and two independent PT1000 at DC+ and DC- of its CCS2 inlet, so A and B often stand for two different contacts.
s: Charging refused or stopped
Charge indicator shows a fault
c: Loose low-voltage connector between inlet and charger
Damaged sensor wire in the inlet harness
Failed sensor element B (usually means a new inlet)

P0EE8.d: P0EE8 is set when sensor B in the charging inlet delivers an electrically valid value that does not fit the situation. A plausibility test may compare it with sensor A on the neighbouring pin, with the outside temperature after a long rest, or with the heating expected for the charge current.
s: Charging reduced or aborted
Fault only at certain stations
c: Worn station plug heating one contact unevenly
Sensor B lost thermal contact to its pin

P0EE9.d: P0EE9 reports that the voltage of coupler temperature sensor B lies under its valid window. What that means thermally depends on the element.
s: Charging not started or stopped
Reduced charging power
c: Sensor B signal wire shorted to ground
Moisture or water in the charging inlet

P0EEA.d: P0EEA is the opposite case: the sensor B signal of the charging inlet sits above the valid window. In a pull-up design that is what an unplugged connector, a broken sensor wire or a short to a supply voltage looks like.
s: Charging aborted at once or refused
Fault in the charge indicator
c: Unplugged connector or broken sensor B wire
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Open sensor element B inside the inlet

P0EEB.d: P0EEB catches a sensor B signal from the charging inlet that jumps or drops out for moments. A metal contact and its plastic housing have real thermal mass, so a change of many degrees within milliseconds cannot be a true temperature and points to the circuit.
s: Charging stops sporadically
Fault cannot be reproduced at once
c: Loose contact in the sensor B circuit or at the charger plug
Moisture that comes and goes in the inlet connector
Cracked sensor element with temperature-dependent contact

P0EEC.d: P0EEC says a second battery energy control module, B, has failed its own internal checks. Large or split packs can carry more than one such controller, each watching cell voltages, temperatures and current of its part.
s: MIL or hybrid warning on
Limited electric drive or charging
c: Software fault or watchdog reset in module B
Low or unstable 12 V supply to the module
Internal hardware fault of module B

P0EED.d: P0EED concerns the active discharge path on the high-voltage side, the circuit that drains the DC link capacitors once the contactors have opened so that no dangerous voltage lingers. The code says this path does not perform as intended, whereas P0C76 only judges how long the voltage takes to fall.
s: MIL or hybrid system warning on
Loss of propulsion or vehicle will not enter ready mode
Further high-voltage codes such as P0C76 or P0C77 stored at the same time
c: Loose or arcing high-voltage cable terminal at the inverter module (FCA 08-107-17)
Discharge resistor or its switching transistor open or degraded
Internal fault in the inverter or its voltage measurement
Main contactor sticking closed so the bus stays charged

P0EEE.d: P0EEE is the overheating verdict for the second measuring point of the charging inlet: sensor B works electrically, but the contact it watches has become too hot, so charging is throttled or stopped. Electrical faults of sensor B have their own codes P0EE7 to P0EEB; overheating at point A is P0E5F, at points C and D P2E4E and P2E53.
s: DC fast charging stops or does not start
Charging power reduced while AC charging still works
Charging fault message in the cluster or app
c: Software of the charging diagnostic module misjudging the temperature (Ford SSM 55080)
Worn, dirty or corroded pins in the charging inlet
Loose crimp or screw connection behind the inlet pin raising contact resistance
Worn plug of the charging station heating the contact

P0EEF.d: P0EEF reports that the control module of drive motor A, the inverter electronics that switch the motor phases, has run too hot. The temperature reading itself is considered valid; faults of the inverter temperature sensors, such as P0AEF, are separate codes.
s: Reduced drive power or hybrid system warning
MIL on (manufacturer-dependent)
Electric drive switched off until the module cools
c: Low coolant level or air in the power electronics cooling loop
Electronics coolant pump weak or failed
Long full-load operation such as towing or climbing in high ambient heat
Degraded power semiconductors or thermal interface inside the module

P0EF0.d: P0EF0 describes a safety lockout rather than a broken actuator: the vehicle keeps the charging connector locked because it still measures hazardous voltage at the inlet. CharIN's CCS design guide permits unlocking only below 60 V, and EVgo's interoperability guide for vehicle makers asks for release once current is close to zero, the inlet is under 60 V DC and the station has changed to state B1.
s: Charging cable cannot be unplugged after charging
Charging fault message, sometimes only at certain stations
Emergency release of the connector needed
c: DC charging contactor stuck closed, inlet stays connected to the battery
Charging station does not switch off or discharge its output
Faulty inlet voltage measurement reporting voltage that is not there
Charging control software ending the session in the wrong order

P0EF1.d: P0EF1 is the general circuit code for the temperature sensor of drive motor C, the third traction motor on vehicles with three or more electric machines. It must not be confused with P2DB1, which means sensor C inside drive motor A.
s: Reduced drive power
Warning lamp for the electric drive
Motor temperature shown as invalid in the scan tool
c: Loose, corroded or damaged connector of the motor C temperature sensor
Temperature sensor in the winding failed
Controller configuration not matching the installed motor (Volvo RD21-022)

P0EF2.d: P0EF2 flags a plausibility error of the drive motor C temperature sensor: its signal is electrically fine, yet the value does not fit what the controller expects. No manufacturer documents P0EF2 publicly.
s: Warning lamp after a long standstill, often at the first start of the day
Usually no noticeable drivability change at first
Power limitation of motor C in some cases
c: Sensor no longer in thermal contact with the winding
Corroded pin adding resistance and shifting the reading
Comparison sensor such as coolant or oil temperature reading wrong

P0EF3.d: P0EF3 is stored when the signal voltage of the drive motor C temperature sensor drops below its valid range. With the usual NTC thermistor on a pull-up resistor, a low voltage stands for an extremely hot winding, so electrically the suspects are a short to ground, a pinched harness or a sensor with an internal short.
s: Drive power of motor C reduced immediately
Implausibly high motor temperature in the live data
Warning lamp on
c: Signal wire shorted to ground or motor housing
Water or coolant in the connector bridging the pins

P0EF4.d: P0EF4 reports a drive motor C temperature signal above the plausible window. For an NTC sensor on a pull-up this equals an impossibly cold winding, the picture produced by an open sensor, a broken wire, an unplugged connector or a short to the reference voltage.
s: Reduced power of motor C
Motor temperature stuck at the lowest value in the live data
Warning lamp on
c: Sensor connector unplugged, loose or with pushed-back pin
Broken signal or ground wire of the sensor
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference

P0EF5.d: P0EF5 covers a drive motor C temperature signal that jumps or drops out for short moments instead of staying wrong. Because of the thermal mass of a traction motor, the winding temperature can only change slowly; a step of many degrees within milliseconds therefore points to the wiring and not to the motor.
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Short power interruptions of motor C, often on rough roads
Jumping motor temperature in the live data
c: Loose or corroded pins in the motor connector
Harness chafing at brackets or moving parts
Cracked sensor lead inside the motor that opens with vibration or heat

P0EF6.d: P0EF6 is not an electrical fault: the drive motor C temperature sensor delivers a believable value, but that value has passed the motor's protection limit. No manufacturer documents P0EF6 publicly.
s: Clearly reduced power until the motor has cooled down
Warning about drive system overheating
MIL on (manufacturer-dependent)
c: Low coolant or oil level, or air in the motor cooling circuit
Failed coolant or oil pump, or clogged cooler
Long full-load phases such as towing, track use or steep climbs
Shorted turns in the stator winding generating extra heat

P0EF7.d: P0EF7 stands for an electrical fault in the second input voltage sensor of on-board charger A, the measuring channel that reads the AC supply voltage coming from a wallbox, station or household outlet. Chargers designed for several phases or split-phase supply may carry more than one such channel; the first one, sensor A, uses P0D3D to P0D41.
s: AC charging does not start or stops shortly after start
Charging fault message in the cluster or app
DC fast charging usually unaffected
c: Fault in the voltage sensing stage inside the charger
Open or high-resistance signal line between sensor and controller
Corroded low-voltage connector at the charger

P0EF8.d: P0EF8 is set when input voltage sensor B of charger A delivers a value that is electrically valid but wrong for the situation. No manufacturer documents P0EF8 publicly.
s: AC charging interrupted or slower than expected
Code may set while driving without any charging attempt
Charging fault message
c: Offset drift of the voltage sensing electronics in the charger
Partial internal fault of the charger input stage
Charger software misjudging the plausibility window

P0EF9.d: P0EF9 means the signal of input voltage sensor B in charger A has fallen below its valid range. No manufacturer documents P0EF9 publicly.
s: AC charging refused
Charging fault message right after plugging in
DC fast charging usually still possible
c: Missing supply voltage of the sensing circuit
Internal fault of the charger measuring stage

P0EFA.d: With P0EFA, the signal from the second input voltage sensor of charger A, sensor B, lies above the plausible window. No manufacturer documents P0EFA publicly.
s: AC charging refused or ends after a few seconds
Charging fault message
Indicated charging power implausible
c: Defective measuring stage on the charger board
Open signal line pulled high by the input circuit
Signal shorted to a supply voltage

P0EFB.d: P0EFB flags an electrical fault on the third AC input voltage channel of on-board charger A, sensor C. Channel A reports through P0D3D to P0D41, channel B through P0EF7 to P0EFA; a third channel fits chargers that read each phase of a three-phase supply separately.
s: AC charging does not start or is limited
Possible reduced charging power on three-phase stations
Charging fault shown in the cluster or app
c: Failed measuring channel C on the charger board (divider, amplifier or converter input)
Open or loose sense connection for this phase inside the charger or at the AC inlet harness
Charger software marking a valid channel as faulty

P0EFC.d: With P0EFC, sensor C of charger A delivers an electrically sound signal whose value conflicts with the charger's other readings. No manufacturer documents P0EFC publicly.
s: Charging stops part-way or does not reach full charge
Fault appears only at certain outlets or stations
Charging fault message, sometimes with a warning lamp
c: Voltage dips, brown-out or power cut at the outlet or station during charging (GM PIC5803 for the sensor A code)
Faulty or poorly calibrated charging cord set or wallbox
Gain or offset drift of measuring channel C in the charger

P0EFD.d: P0EFD reports that the reading of input voltage sensor C in charger A sits below its plausible band. No manufacturer documents P0EFD publicly.
s: AC charging refused right after plugging in
Charging works on a different station or outlet
Charging fault message
c: One phase missing at the supply (tripped breaker or fault in the station or cable)
Sense path of channel C shorted to ground
Defective divider or converter input for channel C in the charger

P0EFE.d: P0EFE is stored when channel C of charger A reports more input voltage than a household or station supply can deliver. No manufacturer documents P0EFE publicly.
s: AC charging stops within seconds of starting
Displayed supply voltage unrealistically high
Charging fault message
c: Open lower resistor in the voltage divider of channel C
Sense signal shorted to the converter reference or a supply rail
Actual overvoltage or surge from the supply
